rules.flag: Asks for payment in gift cards
rules.explain: No real company, bank, store, or government agency accepts gift cards as payment for bills, fees, fines, or refunds. If gift cards are the payment method, it is a scam. Every time.

rules.flag: Involves cryptocurrency
rules.explain: Legitimate banks, agencies, and stores do not ask you to pay, invest, or move money through crypto in a text, call, or chat. Crypto payments are nearly impossible to reverse, which is exactly why scammers demand them.

rules.flag: Asks you to wire or mail money
rules.explain: Wiring money or mailing cash is like handing someone an envelope on the street - once it is gone, it is gone. Real debts and real fees never have to be paid this way.

rules.flag: Tells you to keep it secret or stay on the line
rules.explain: Scammers need you isolated. A real bank, agency, or family emergency never requires secrecy, and no legitimate caller forbids you from hanging up and calling back on a number you trust.

rules.flag: Threatens arrest or legal action
rules.explain: Government agencies do not call people and threaten arrest over a payment. Threats are used to make you panic and pay before you think.

rules.flag: Threatens to close, lock, or cut off something
rules.explain: Shutoff and lockout threats with minutes to act are a pressure trick. Real closures come with written notice and time to respond.

rules.flag: Pushes you to act right now
rules.explain: Urgency is the scammer's main tool - it stops you from checking. Anything real can survive you taking ten minutes to verify it.

rules.flag: Asks for a security code sent to your phone
rules.explain: That code is the key to your account. Banks say it in the message itself: they will NEVER ask for it. Anyone who asks for the code is trying to log in as you.

rules.flag: Asks for remote access to your device
rules.explain: Letting a stranger connect to your phone or computer gives them your banking apps, passwords, and files. No support company works this way from an incoming call or popup.

phrases: you have been selected to receive
rules.flag: Says you won a prize or lottery
rules.explain: You cannot win a contest you never entered, real sweepstakes never charge winners fees, and foreign lotteries are illegal in the US. Prize-plus-a-fee is always a scam.

rules.flag: Promises guaranteed investment profits
rules.explain: Real investments can lose money, so nobody honest guarantees returns. Guaranteed profits are the bait in nearly every investment scam the FTC warns about.

rules.flag: Demands a fee to release money, a prize, or a package
rules.explain: Paying a fee to unlock money that is supposedly yours is the oldest trick in fraud. Real refunds, prizes, wages, and deliveries do not work this way.

rules.flag: Asks you to verify account details through the message
rules.explain: Verification requests belong inside the official app or website that YOU open - never through a link, reply, or caller that contacted you first.

rules.flag: Tells you to move money to keep it safe
rules.explain: Banks never ask customers to move money to a 'safe account.' That instruction is the theft itself - the 'safe' account belongs to the scammer.

rules.flag: Runs a refund or cancellation by phone
rules.explain: Fake renewal and invoice scams funnel you into calling a 'refund department' that will try for remote access or a fake over-refund. Real refunds never need either.

rules.flag: Family emergency asking for bail or rescue money
rules.explain: The grandparent scam runs on love and panic - a relative 'in trouble' plus a stranger handling the money. Always verify by calling your family member on the number you already have.

rules.flag: Easy-money job that may ask you to deposit first
rules.explain: A real job pays you; it never charges you. Task scams pay small amounts at first as bait, then take much larger 'unlock' deposits.

rules.flag: Overpayment that needs a partial refund
rules.explain: The overpayment is fake - a forged check or screenshot. Your 'refund' of the difference is real money leaving your account before the bank catches up.

rules.flag: Asks you to confirm a purchase by replying
rules.explain: Real banks send messages like this - and scammers copy them word for word, because your reply tells them you are engaged and a phone call comes next. The wording alone cannot prove which one this is. The safe move is identical either way: do not reply, and call the number on the back of your card.

phrases: number on the back of your card
rules.flag: Good sign: it points you to the number on your own card
rules.explain: Telling you to call the number printed on your card is what real banks do - a scammer wants you calling THEIR number instead. This lowers the score, but it does not erase other red flags.

rules.flag: Fake-check job setup (equipment or vendor payment)
rules.explain: Real employers never mail you a check to buy equipment from 'their' vendor. The check bounces days later - after you have sent the 'vendor' (the scammer) real money from your own account.

rules.flag: Advance-fee setup (the 'foreign prince' pattern)
rules.explain: A stranger with a fortune needs your help moving or receiving money - and offers you a cut. The fortune does not exist. The real goal is the 'small fee' or the bank details they ask for next, and every fee you pay invents another one.

rules.flag: Asks for your banking information
rules.explain: No bank, agency, or real company asks for your account number, routing number, card PIN, or banking password by text, email, or phone message. Anyone asking for these is setting up to take money out, not put money in.

rules.flag: Asks you to send money
rules.explain: Sending money is the one thing every scam on this list is trying to get you to do - and it is also something friends and family occasionally ask for. What decides it is WHO is asking and whether the story checks out. If the request is unexpected, from a stranger, or comes with any pressure, treat it as a scam and verify the person through a number you already have.

rules.flag: Asks for your banking, login, or personal information
rules.explain: The wording pairs an ask (send, share, confirm, enter) with something no real bank or agency ever requests by message: account details, a password, a PIN, a login code, or your Social Security or Medicare number. The exact words do not matter - the pairing is the scam.

rules.flag: Asks you to send money
rules.explain: Sending money is the one thing every scam on this list is trying to get you to do - and it is also something friends and family occasionally ask for. What decides it is WHO is asking and whether the story checks out. If the request is unexpected, from a stranger, or comes with any pressure, treat it as a scam and verify the person through a number you already have.

scams.name: Fake USPS Package Text
scams.summary: A text claims a package cannot be delivered and asks you to pay a tiny 'redelivery fee' or fix your address through a link. The link opens a fake USPS site that steals your card details - the small fee is just the hook.
scams.example: USPS: Your package is on hold due to an incomplete address. Update your info and pay the $0.30 redelivery fee here: usps-redelivery[.]com
redFlags: USPS does not text about packages unless you signed up for tracking alerts
Real USPS redelivery is free - there is no fee
The link is not usps.com
Pressure to fix it today or lose the package
whatToDo: Do not tap the link
Check tracking yourself at usps.com
If you paid, call your card company and dispute the charge, then watch for more charges
Forward the text to 7726 (SPAM) to report it

scams.name: Unpaid Toll Text (SunPass / E-ZPass)
scams.summary: A text says you owe a small unpaid toll and threatens a big late fee or a suspended license unless you pay through a link right now. Toll agencies do not collect this way, and the payment site is fake - it steals your card.
scams.example: SunPass: You have an outstanding toll balance of $6.99. To avoid a $50 late fee, pay now: sunpass-pay[.]online
redFlags: A huge late fee threatened over a tiny toll
The link is not sunpass.com or your official toll site
You have not driven that road recently
The text comes from a random number or an email address
whatToDo: Type sunpass.com yourself and check your real account
Delete the text - real toll bills arrive by mail or in your account
If you paid, dispute it with your card company

scams.name: Fake Bank Fraud Department
scams.summary: A text or call claims to be your bank's fraud department asking about a charge you never made. When you engage, they walk you into 'verifying' yourself or moving money to a 'safe account' - which is their account. Imposter scams are the most reported scam in America, and bank imposters are the biggest text version.
scams.example: CHASE FRAUD ALERT: Did you attempt a $1,850 purchase at Best Buy? Reply YES or NO and an agent will call you shortly.
redFlags: They ask for your PIN, password, or a code that was texted to you - a real bank never does
They tell you to move money to keep it safe
They rush you and warn you not to call the bank yourself
The caller ID shows your bank's number - that can be faked
whatToDo: Do not reply - hang up
Call the number on the back of your card yourself
Never move money because a caller told you to
If you sent money, call your bank immediately and ask for the fraud department

scams.name: IRS Tax Debt Call
scams.summary: A caller claims you owe back taxes and will be arrested or sued unless you pay today - usually in gift cards, crypto, or a wire. The IRS sends letters first and never demands instant payment by phone.
scams.example: This is the IRS. A lawsuit has been filed against you for tax fraud. Call us back immediately or a warrant will be issued for your arrest.
redFlags: Threats of arrest - the IRS does not work this way
Payment demanded in gift cards, wire, or crypto
First contact by phone instead of by mail
They will not let you hang up and verify
whatToDo: Hang up
If you are worried, call the IRS yourself at 1-800-829-1040
Report the call at reportfraud.ftc.gov

scams.name: Social Security Suspension Call
scams.summary: A caller says your Social Security number has been 'suspended' or linked to a crime, and that you must verify information or move money to protect your benefits. Social Security numbers are never suspended, and the SSA does not call people like this.
scams.example: Your Social Security number has been suspended due to suspicious activity. Press 1 to speak to an officer before legal action begins.
redFlags: A 'suspended' Social Security number - there is no such thing
Threats of arrest or losing benefits
Asked to buy gift cards to 'secure' your number
A robocall that asks you to press 1
whatToDo: Hang up - just hang up
Call Social Security yourself at 1-800-772-1213 if you are concerned
Report it to the Social Security fraud hotline: 1-800-269-0271
signatures: social security number has been suspended

scams.name: Medicare Card and Benefits Scam
scams.summary: A caller offers a 'new plastic Medicare card,' a free medical brace, or a benefits review, then asks for your Medicare number. That number is the prize - it gets used to bill Medicare for equipment you never received.
scams.example: We are issuing new plastic Medicare cards this month. I just need to verify your Medicare number so we can mail yours out.
redFlags: Medicare never calls to 'verify' your number
There is no card rollout that requires a phone call
Free braces, tests, or equipment offered out of the blue
They know a little about you and fish for the rest
whatToDo: Never give your Medicare number to someone who called you
Hang up and call Medicare yourself at 1-800-633-4227
Check your Medicare statements for equipment you never got

scams.name: Grandparent / Family Emergency Scam
scams.summary: A caller pretends to be your grandchild, your child, or their lawyer: 'I'm in jail,' 'I'm in the hospital,' 'send money - and please don't tell Mom and Dad.' Scammers can now clone a family member's voice from a few seconds of audio. The secrecy and the urgency are the tell.
scams.example: Grandma? It's me - I'm in trouble, I was in an accident and I'm at the police station. Please don't tell Mom, just send the bail money.
redFlags: 'Don't tell anyone' - real emergencies do not need secrecy
Money by wire, gift card, or a courier picking up cash
A 'lawyer' or 'officer' takes over the call
They dodge questions only the real person could answer
whatToDo: Hang up and call your family member on the number you already have
Agree on a family code word for real emergencies
Never send money based on a single phone call

scams.name: Tech Support Popup and Call Scam
scams.summary: A full-screen popup (or an unexpected call) claims your computer is infected and gives you a number to call. The 'technician' asks for remote access, 'finds' problems, and charges you - and may plant real malware or steal banking logins while connected.
scams.example: WARNING! Your computer has been blocked due to a virus. Call Microsoft Support immediately at 1-8XX-XXX-XXXX. Do not shut down your computer.
redFlags: Microsoft and Apple never put phone numbers in error messages
'Do not shut down' - shutting down is exactly the safe move
They ask you to install remote-access software
Payment demanded in gift cards
whatToDo: Close the browser or restart the computer - never call the number
Never give a stranger remote access to your devices
If you paid, call your card company
If you installed their software, have a local repair shop clean the machine

scams.name: Fake Antivirus Renewal (Geek Squad / Norton)
scams.summary: An email says your antivirus subscription renewed for $299-$499 and gives a number to call to cancel. There is no charge - the call is the trap. The 'refund agent' asks for remote access or a refund form, then fakes an over-refund and demands the difference back in gift cards.
scams.example: Your Geek Squad subscription has been renewed for $389.99. If you did not authorize this charge, call us within 24 hours to cancel.
redFlags: You do not have that subscription
The email comes from a Gmail-style address, not the company
A scary charge amount with a tight cancel deadline
The 'refund' needs your bank login or remote access
whatToDo: Check your real bank or card statement - there is almost never a charge
Do not call the number in the email
If you called and gave access, shut the computer down and call your bank

scams.name: PayPal Invoice Scam
scams.summary: You get a real-looking PayPal invoice or 'payment confirmed' email for something expensive you never bought, with a phone number to dispute it. The number is not PayPal - the 'agent' runs the fake-refund or remote-access play from there.
scams.example: Payment of $699.99 to Bitcoin Exchange confirmed via PayPal. If this was not you, call PayPal support immediately: 1-8XX-XXX-XXXX.
redFlags: The support number only exists inside the message - real PayPal disputes happen inside paypal.com
It pressures you to call fast
Crypto appears in a 'purchase' you never made
whatToDo: Log in at paypal.com yourself - never through the email's link - and look; the charge usually is not there
Never call a phone number from an invoice email
Delete it once you have confirmed your account is fine

scams.name: Fake Amazon Account Alert
scams.summary: A text or email says your Amazon account is locked, or a suspicious order has shipped, and links to a pixel-perfect fake Amazon login page. Type your password there and they own your account - and the card saved on it.
scams.example: Amazon: Your account has been locked due to unusual sign-in activity. Verify your account within 24 hours: amzn-verify[.]com
redFlags: The link is not amazon.com
'Locked unless you act within 24 hours' urgency
The page asks for your full card number - Amazon does not do that on a login page
whatToDo: Open the Amazon app or type amazon.com yourself and check your account there
Turn on two-step verification in your real account
If you entered your password on the fake page, change it immediately

scams.name: Romance Scam
scams.summary: Someone met on a dating site or social media builds a relationship over weeks - always with a reason they can never meet: military deployment, overseas work, an oil rig. Then comes the emergency: customs fees, a plane ticket, a medical bill, or a can't-miss investment. The person in the photos is not the person typing.
scams.example: You know I would be there if I could, my love. The deployment keeps getting extended. I just need help with the paperwork fee so I can come home to you.
redFlags: Can never video call or meet in person
Falls in love fast and intensely
Money requests start small and keep growing
Asks for gift cards, wire transfers, or crypto
whatToDo: Stop sending money - every dollar sent is gone
Reverse-image-search their photos; they are usually stolen
Talk to a friend or family member about it - secrecy is the scammer's tool
Report the profile on the app where you met

scams.name: Crypto Investment Scam (Pig Butchering)
scams.summary: A friendly stranger - often starting as a 'wrong number' text or a dating match - chats for weeks, then casually mentions making money in crypto and offers to teach you. A fake trading app shows your balance growing... until you try to withdraw and must pay 'taxes' or 'fees' first. The app is fake and every dollar is gone.
scams.example: My uncle works at an investment firm - he taught me a strategy that has been making me 20% a month. I can walk you through your first trade. Start small.
redFlags: Investment tips from someone you met online and never in person
Guaranteed or suspiciously steady high returns
Withdrawals blocked until you pay extra fees
Pressure to keep it secret and to invest more
whatToDo: Never invest on a tip from an online-only friend
If money is in, do NOT pay withdrawal 'fees' - that is the second bite
Save all messages and report it to the FBI at ic3.gov

scams.name: Wrong-Number Text Scam
scams.summary: An innocent-looking text - 'Hi Sarah, are we still on for Saturday?' - is not a mistake. Replying starts a friendly conversation designed to become a friendship, then a romance or a crypto pitch. It is the front door to the romance and pig-butchering scams.
scams.example: Hi, is this Dr. Lee's office? ... Oh, I'm so sorry, wrong number! You seem kind though - what do you do?
redFlags: The 'stranger' keeps the conversation going after the mistake
Quickly suggests moving to WhatsApp or Telegram
Wealthy lifestyle photos and a glamorous job
Eventually mentions investing or asks for money
whatToDo: Do not engage - just delete it
A real wrong number does not need a reply
Never move a stranger to another messaging app

scams.name: Fake Job / Task Scam
scams.summary: A text or WhatsApp message offers easy money for simple online 'tasks' - liking videos, rating products, boosting orders. Small payments arrive at first to build trust; then you must deposit your own money to 'unlock' bigger tasks. The deposits vanish. Losses to this scam have reached tens of millions of dollars a year.
scams.example: Earn $100-$300/day from your phone! Simple product-boosting tasks, 30 minutes a day. Reply YES to start.
redFlags: The job found you by random text
You must pay or deposit money in order to earn
Pay is handled in crypto
No real interview, company website, or paperwork
whatToDo: Never pay to get paid - a real job never charges you
Stop depositing; the early 'earnings' were bait
Report it at reportfraud.ftc.gov

scams.name: Marketplace Overpayment / Fake Buyer
scams.summary: Selling something online? A 'buyer' sends a check or a payment screenshot for MORE than your price and asks you to refund the difference - or sends a fake payment email claiming you must 'upgrade to a business account' first. The payment is fake; your refund is real.
scams.example: I sent $850 for the $600 couch - my mover's fee is included. Please Zelle $250 to the mover and keep the rest for your trouble.
redFlags: Overpayment of any kind, for any reason
Payment by check or screenshot instead of inside the app
They cannot meet in person
They rush you to ship or refund before the payment 'clears'
whatToDo: Accept payment only inside the app, or cash in person
Never refund an overpayment - the overpayment IS the scam
If a check arrived, wait for your bank to confirm it truly cleared - that takes days, not hours
signatures: keep the rest for your trouble

scams.name: Puppy and Pet Deposit Scam
scams.summary: A website or social post advertises adorable puppies at too-good prices. You pay a deposit, then a shipping fee, then 'insurance,' then a special crate fee - each one urgent, each one 'the last.' There is no puppy. This scam steals millions from people at their most hopeful.
scams.example: Your puppy is ready! We just need the $150 refundable crate fee before she can be shipped to you tomorrow.
redFlags: Price far below normal for the breed
Seller will not video-call with the actual puppy or let you visit
Payment by gift card, Zelle, or wire only
New 'fees' keep appearing after you pay
whatToDo: Buy only from a breeder you can visit, or video-call live with the actual puppy
Never pay pet deposits by gift card or wire
Reverse-image-search the puppy photos - they are usually stolen from real breeders

scams.name: Boss / Gift Card Request
scams.summary: An email or text that looks like it is from your boss, pastor, or club president asks you to quietly buy gift cards for a client surprise or staff reward and send the numbers. It is not them - and 'don't tell anyone, it's a surprise' is doing the heavy lifting.
scams.example: Are you at the store? I need 4 x $100 Apple gift cards for a client emergency. Keep it between us - I will reimburse you today. Send me the card numbers when you have them.
redFlags: Gift cards requested by email or text instead of in person
Secrecy - 'it's a surprise'
The sender's address is almost, but not quite, the real one
You are asked to scratch off and send the card numbers
whatToDo: Call or walk over to the person and ask - 30 seconds kills this scam
Never send gift card numbers to anyone
If you bought cards, call the number on the back right away - unspent balances can sometimes be frozen

scams.name: Prize, Lottery, and Sweepstakes Scam
scams.summary: You have 'won' a lottery, a sweepstakes, or a Publishers Clearing House prize - you just need to pay taxes or fees first, usually in gift cards or by wire. Real sweepstakes never make winners pay to collect, and it is illegal for foreign lotteries to sell tickets to Americans at all.
scams.example: Congratulations! You've won $1.5 million and a new Mercedes from Publishers Clearing House! To release your prize, pay the $499 processing tax today.
redFlags: You must pay to receive a prize - always fake
You never entered that lottery
Secrecy: 'don't tell family until it is finalized'
Payment in gift cards, wire, or cash by mail
whatToDo: Hang up or delete it - real PCH shows up at your door with cameras and never asks for money
Never pay a fee to claim a prize
Report it at reportfraud.ftc.gov

scams.name: Utility Shutoff Scam
scams.summary: A caller claims to be your power or water company: your bill is overdue and a crew is on the way to shut you off within the hour unless you pay right now - in gift cards, Zelle, or at a payment kiosk. Real utilities send written notices and never demand instant payment this way.
scams.example: This is Duke Energy. Your account is scheduled for disconnection in 45 minutes. To stop it, pay $212 now - do not hang up.
redFlags: A shutoff threat with minutes to act
Payment demanded by gift card, Zelle, or kiosk
They tell you not to hang up or call the company yourself
The caller knows your address - that is public information, not proof
whatToDo: Hang up and call the number printed on your real utility bill
Check your account on the company's real website yourself
Remember: real shutoffs come with written notice days ahead - never a 45-minute phone deadline

scams.name: The Foreign Prince / Inheritance Scam
scams.summary: The oldest email scam there is, still working after 40 years. A 'prince,' royal, oil executive, dying widow, or foreign official has millions they must move out of their country in secret, and they have chosen YOU to receive it - for a generous cut. There is no fortune. They want an upfront 'release' or 'transfer' fee, or your bank details, and each payment invents another problem that needs another fee.
scams.example: Dear trusted friend, I am a Saudi prince and a member of the royal family. I must transfer $42 million dollars out of my country in secret, and I need a foreign partner to receive the funds. You will keep 30 percent for your help. Please send your bank account details and a $500 release fee. This is completely risk free.
redFlags: A stranger offers you a cut of millions for almost no work
Royalty, a dying widow, a refugee, or an official who 'found' your name
Secrecy: the money must move quietly, tell no one
An upfront fee - release, transfer, legal, or clearance - before you see a cent
Requests your bank account details to 'send' you money
Poorly written formality: barristers, consignment boxes, trunk boxes of cash
scams.whatToDo: Do not reply at all - replying marks you as a live target and the stories and pressure escalate. Never pay any fee and never share bank details. Real inheritances come through probate courts and lawyers you can verify independently, never through a stranger's email.

scams.example: This is Sergeant Miller with the County Sheriff's Department. Our records show you failed to appear for jury duty and a warrant has been issued. Pay the $850 civil assessment fee by phone now or deputies will come to your home to arrest you.
scams.name: Fake Jury Duty Call
redFlags: Threat of arrest for missing jury duty
Demands payment by phone right now
Wants gift cards, Zelle, or a wire transfer
Tells you not to hang up or call anyone
Caller ID appears to show a real sheriff or court number
scams.summary: A caller claiming to be from the courthouse or sheriff's office says you missed jury duty and a warrant is out for your arrest. They say you can avoid jail by paying a fine right now over the phone, usually with gift cards or a payment app. Real courts never demand instant payment by phone to cancel an arrest warrant.
whatToDo: Hang up. Courts send jury notices by mail, never pay-by-phone threats.
Call the courthouse yourself using the number on its official website.
Never pay a 'fine' with gift cards or payment apps.
Report the call to your local sheriff's non-emergency line.

scams.example: Deputy Harris, County Sheriff's Office. A bench warrant was issued in your name this morning. You can resolve it today by paying $1,200 through our payment line at 1-800-555-0147. If we don't hear from you within two hours, officers will be dispatched to your address.
scams.name: Fake Arrest Warrant Call
redFlags: Says a warrant was issued in your name
Payment demanded within hours
Refuses to let you come to the station in person
Wants payment by gift card, wire, or crypto
Warns you not to tell anyone about the call
scams.summary: Someone posing as a sheriff's deputy says a warrant has been issued for your arrest and you must pay today to clear it. The goal is to panic you into sending money before you have time to check. Law enforcement never calls ahead to collect warrant payments by phone.
whatToDo: Hang up and do not call the number they gave you.
Look up your sheriff's real number and ask about any warrant yourself.
Remember: police never take warrant payments over the phone.
Report the call to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov.

scams.example: This is Agent Collins with the FBI. Your Social Security number was found connected to a money laundering case in Texas. To protect your funds, you must transfer your savings to a secure federal account today and keep this matter confidential.
scams.name: Fake FBI Agent Call
redFlags: Claims your SSN was used in a crime
Tells you to move money to a 'safe' account
Demands secrecy — do not tell your bank or family
Threatens arrest or asset seizure if you refuse
Asks for your full SSN, bank logins, or account numbers
scams.summary: A caller claims to be an FBI agent and says your Social Security number or bank account was used in drug trafficking, money laundering, or another serious crime. They pressure you to 'verify' your identity or move your money to a 'protected' account. The FBI never calls people to demand money or personal details this way.
whatToDo: Hang up. The FBI does not clear crimes over the phone.
Never move money because a caller told you to.
Call your bank using the number on your card if you are worried.
Report it to the FBI at ic3.gov.

scams.example: U.S. Customs and Border Protection: A parcel addressed to you was intercepted at the port of entry containing illegal items. To avoid criminal charges, pay the $640 clearance fee at cbp-releasepay.com within 24 hours.
scams.name: Customs Package Seizure Scam
redFlags: Claims a package in your name was seized
Fee demanded to release or clear the package
Link or phone number provided for instant payment
Hints at drugs or illegal contents to scare you
Deadline of hours, not days
scams.summary: You get a call or text saying U.S. Customs and Border Protection seized a package with your name on it — sometimes claiming it contained drugs or cash. They demand a release or clearance fee, or your personal information, to 'resolve' it. CBP does not collect fees by phone or text for seized packages.
whatToDo: Do not pay and do not click the link.
Real customs notices arrive by mail with a case you can verify.
Contact CBP through the official cbp.gov website.
Report the message to the FTC.

scams.example: This is Officer Grant from U.S. Immigration. There is a discrepancy in your file and a deportation order is pending. You must pay a $2,400 administrative bond today by phone and provide your passport number to stop removal proceedings.
scams.name: Immigration Threat Scam
redFlags: Threatens deportation or arrest today
Demands a bond or fee paid by phone
Asks for passport or A-number on the spot
Insists the problem be kept secret
Caller pressures you to stay on the line
scams.summary: A caller claims to be from ICE or U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and says there is a problem with your immigration status. They threaten arrest or deportation unless you pay a fee or hand over personal information immediately. Real immigration agencies do not demand instant payment by phone to stop deportation.
whatToDo: Hang up. USCIS and ICE do not collect bond payments by cold call.
Check any real case at uscis.gov using your own receipt number.
Talk to a licensed immigration attorney before paying anything.
Report the call to the FTC.

scams.example: FL DMV Alert: Our records show an unpaid violation on your license. Your driving privilege will be suspended in 48 hours. Pay the $38.00 fee now to avoid suspension: fl-dmv-payfees.com
scams.name: DMV License Suspension Text
redFlags: License suspension threat by text message
Small fee with a payment link
Web address that is not the official state DMV site
Urgent 24-48 hour deadline
Asks for card number and driver's license details
scams.summary: A text claims your driving privilege or license will be suspended unless you pay an outstanding fee through the link provided. The link leads to a fake DMV page built to steal your card details and personal information. State DMVs do not send license suspension threats by text with payment links.
whatToDo: Do not tap the link in the text.
Go to your state's official DMV website by typing the address yourself.
Check your license status there or call the DMV directly.
Forward scam texts to 7726 (SPAM).

scams.example: NOTICE OF TAX LIEN: County records show $4,317.62 in delinquent property taxes on your home. To prevent a lien and forced sale, remit payment within 10 days by calling our collections office at 1-800-555-0123.
scams.name: Property Tax Lien Scam
redFlags: Sudden claim of large back taxes owed
Threat of a lien or forced home sale
Payment demanded by phone or wire
Letter has no parcel or account number you recognize
Refuses to accept payment through the county office
scams.summary: You receive an official-looking letter, call, or text claiming you owe back property taxes and a lien will be placed on your home unless you pay right away. The scammers copy county letterhead to look convincing. Real tax collectors send mailed notices with months of process before any lien.
whatToDo: Contact your county tax collector using the number on their official website.
Ask for an itemized statement of any taxes actually owed.
Pay property taxes only through official county channels.
Report the letter or call to the FTC.

scams.example: FEMA Disaster Assistance: You qualify for $750 in immediate relief plus housing aid for storm damage. Complete your application today by providing your Social Security number and bank account for direct deposit at fema-relief-claims.com. A $25 processing fee applies.
scams.name: Fake FEMA Relief Scam
redFlags: Aid offered right after a disaster by text or knock on the door
Processing or application fee requested
Asks for SSN and bank details upfront
'FEMA worker' has no official photo ID badge
Website is not disasterassistance.gov
scams.summary: After a hurricane, flood, or fire, scammers pose as FEMA workers offering disaster aid. They ask for your Social Security number, bank details, or an 'application fee' to process your assistance. Real FEMA aid is free to apply for and never requires a processing fee.
whatToDo: Apply only at disasterassistance.gov or the official FEMA number 1-800-621-3362.
Never pay a fee to apply for disaster aid.
Ask any in-person worker for official FEMA photo ID.
Report fraud to the FEMA Disaster Fraud Hotline.

scams.example: Congratulations! Your business was pre-approved for a $48,000 SBA disaster loan. To release the funds this week, we require a one-time processing fee of $495. Reply YES and our funding team will send your secure payment link.
scams.name: Fake SBA Loan Scam
redFlags: Loan 'pre-approved' without an application
Upfront fee required before funds are released
Pressure to pay today to lock in the loan
Emails from look-alike addresses, not sba.gov
Payment requested by wire or payment app
scams.summary: You are told your business has been approved for a Small Business Administration loan or disaster loan, but you must pay an upfront 'processing' or 'insurance' fee to release the funds. The loan does not exist. The real SBA never charges fees through third parties who call or email you out of the blue.
whatToDo: Apply for SBA loans only through sba.gov.
Never pay a fee to 'release' a loan.
Call the SBA at 1-800-659-2955 to verify any offer.
Report the offer to the FTC.

scams.example: Calling our veterans about an important benefits update. Our review shows you may qualify for a lump-sum pension option or increased compensation. There is a small enrollment fee to process your claim — press 1 to speak with a benefits advisor today.
scams.name: VA Benefits Scam
redFlags: Offers a lump sum in exchange for future pension payments
Charges a fee to file or review a VA claim
Claims a deadline to keep or increase benefits
Adviser is not VA-accredited
Asks for your VA login or bank details by phone
scams.summary: Scammers target veterans with calls about a 'benefits review,' a refund, or buying out their pension for a lump sum. Some charge fees for filing VA claims, which accredited help will do for free, and pension buyouts leave veterans with far less than their benefits are worth. The VA never charges for a benefits review over the phone.
whatToDo: Use a VA-accredited VSO like the VFW, DAV, or American Legion — they help free.
Verify any claim status yourself at va.gov.
Never sign over future pension payments for a lump sum.
Report it to the VA OIG hotline or the FTC.

scams.example: Census Bureau Notice: Your American Community Survey response is incomplete. To avoid a federal penalty, confirm your household information, Social Security number, and bank account for verification at uscensus-verify.com within 7 days.
scams.name: Fake Census Worker Scam
redFlags: Asks for your full Social Security number
Asks for bank account or online passwords
Threatens a fine or arrest for not answering
Website is not census.gov
Worker cannot show an official Census Bureau ID badge
scams.summary: Someone posing as a Census Bureau worker — at your door, by phone, or through a fake website — asks questions that go far beyond the real census, fishing for your Social Security number, bank account, or passwords. Real census workers never ask for your full SSN, bank details, or money.
whatToDo: Real census mailings point only to census.gov — type the address yourself.
Verify a door-to-door worker's ID or call the Census Bureau regional office.
Never give out your full SSN or banking details.
Report the contact to the Census Bureau and the FTC.

scams.example: This is the County Clerk's office. You failed to appear in court on the 14th regarding case #8841 and a fine of $975 is now due. Pay by phone today to avoid a contempt warrant being issued for your arrest.
scams.name: Missed Court Date Scam
redFlags: Court case or hearing you never knew about
Fine due immediately by phone
Threat of contempt warrant or arrest
Will not provide paperwork you can verify
Payment only by gift card, wire, or app
scams.summary: A caller says you missed a court appearance — sometimes about a subpoena or a case you never heard of — and now owe a fine, with arrest if you do not pay immediately by phone. Courts do not collect fines this way. The panic and the deadline are the whole trick.
whatToDo: Hang up and call the courthouse directly using its official number.
Ask the clerk to look up any case under your name.
Never pay a court fine to a caller who contacted you.
Report the call to the FTC.

scams.example: Child Support Enforcement: Our system shows you are $2,140 past due. Your driver's license will be suspended and a warrant issued unless payment is made today. Call 1-800-555-0186 to resolve this balance immediately.
scams.name: Fake Child Support Enforcement Scam
redFlags: Past-due amount you do not recognize
Payment demanded today to stop license suspension
Threats of immediate jail
Payment by gift card, Zelle, or Cash App requested
Caller cannot give your official case number
scams.summary: A scammer posing as child support enforcement claims you are behind on payments and demands money right now, threatening license suspension or jail. Payments are directed to gift cards or payment apps instead of the state disbursement system. Real child support agencies send official notices and never collect through gift cards.
whatToDo: Check your balance through your state's official child support portal or office.
Never pay child support through gift cards or apps.
Ask for written documentation of any amount owed.
Report the call to your state child support agency and the FTC.

scams.example: This is mediation calling about a delinquent account of $1,480 from an unpaid loan. If payment is not received today by prepaid card, we will file suit and notify your employer. This is your final opportunity to settle before legal action.
scams.name: Fake Debt Collector Scam
redFlags: Debt you do not recognize or remember
Threats of arrest or immediate lawsuit
Refuses to mail written proof of the debt
Demands gift cards, prepaid cards, or wire
Won't give the company's real name and address
scams.summary: An aggressive caller insists you owe a debt — often an old payday loan or a bill you never had — and threatens lawsuits or arrest unless you pay now with gift cards or a wire. Real collectors must mail you written proof of the debt and cannot threaten arrest. Refusing to document the debt is the biggest tell.
whatToDo: Ask for a written validation notice — real collectors must send one.
Do not pay anything until you verify the debt is real and yours.
Check your free credit reports at annualcreditreport.com.
Report fake collectors to the FTC and your state attorney general.

scams.example: Attention taxpayers: The IRS Fresh Start program can eliminate up to 90% of your back taxes. Our tax relief team has settled millions for clients just like you. Call now for your free consultation — enrollment requires only a $2,500 retainer to start today.
scams.name: Tax Relief Company Scam
redFlags: Promises to settle tax debt for pennies on the dollar
Large upfront retainer before any work is done
Guarantees the IRS will accept an offer
Pressures you to sign up on the first call
Claims a limited-time 'Fresh Start' enrollment window
scams.summary: Ads and calls promise to settle your IRS debt for 'pennies on the dollar' through a special program. After a large upfront fee — often thousands — the company does little or nothing, and your tax debt, penalties, and interest keep growing. Only the IRS decides who qualifies for a settlement, and very few taxpayers do.
whatToDo: Check settlement options yourself at irs.gov under Offer in Compromise.
The IRS charges a small application fee — never thousands upfront to a middleman.
Get a second opinion from a licensed tax attorney or CPA.
Report misleading tax relief ads to the FTC.

scams.example: U.S. Treasury Notice: Your $1,400 economic relief payment is ready but unclaimed. To receive your funds by direct deposit, verify your bank account and Social Security number within 72 hours: treasury-claimpayment.com
scams.name: Fake Stimulus Payment Scam
redFlags: Government payment that must be 'claimed' by link
Asks for bank account and SSN on a website
Sender or site is not irs.gov or treasury.gov
72-hour deadline to pressure you
Text or email instead of official mail
scams.summary: A text or email says a new government stimulus or economic payment is waiting for you and you must 'claim' it by entering your bank details on a website. There is no payment to claim — the page steals your banking and identity information. Real government payments arrive automatically and never require entering details through a text link.
whatToDo: Do not click the link or enter any details.
Check real payment information only at irs.gov.
Remember stimulus payments never require a claim form by text.
Forward the text to 7726 (SPAM) and delete it.

scams.example: State Benefits Alert: Your unemployment claim requires identity verification to release this week's payment. Upload your driver's license and confirm your Social Security number here: fl-benefits-verify.com — failure to verify within 24 hours will close your claim.
scams.name: Unemployment Benefits Scam
redFlags: Benefits site reached through a text or ad link
Asks to upload ID plus full SSN on an unfamiliar site
Website address is not an official state .gov domain
Threatens to close your claim within 24 hours
Requests a fee to file or speed up a claim
scams.summary: Scammers build fake state unemployment websites and send texts or ads directing you to 'file your claim' or 'verify your benefits.' The fake site harvests your Social Security number, driver's license, and banking details to file fraudulent claims in your name. Always reach your state benefits site from the official state government page.
whatToDo: Go to your state's official workforce or benefits site by typing the .gov address yourself.
Never file a claim through a link in a text or social media ad.
If you entered information, place a fraud alert with a credit bureau.
Report identity theft at identitytheft.gov.

scams.example: Dear beneficiary: Our records show you were overpaid $23,416 in benefits. You must repay this amount within 30 days or your benefits will be terminated and your case referred for prosecution. To resolve immediately, call 1-844-555-0139.
scams.name: Social Security Overpayment Letter Scam
redFlags: Demands repayment by gift card, wire, or cash
Threatens benefit termination or prosecution for instant action
Asks you to call a number that is not on ssa.gov
Real SSA overpayment letters offer appeal and waiver options, not phone settlements
scams.summary: An official-looking letter says Social Security overpaid you thousands and demands repayment fast - sometimes by gift card, wire, or cash - or your benefits stop and prosecution follows. Real overpayment notices do exist, which is what makes this work, but real SSA letters never demand gift cards or same-day payment over the phone.
whatToDo: Do not call the number on the letter
Verify at ssa.gov or call SSA at 1-800-772-1213
If you really owe, SSA offers payment plans and appeals - ask about both
Never repay a government debt with gift cards or wire transfers

scams.example: Great news! You have been selected to receive a $9,000 federal grant that never has to be repaid. To release your grant funds today, simply pay the $180 processing and insurance fee by gift card or wire transfer.
scams.name: Fake Government Grant Scam
redFlags: Grant offered to you without any application
Processing, insurance, or release fee required
Fee payable by gift card or wire
Caller says you were 'selected' or 'chosen'
Money promised the same day
scams.summary: You are told you were 'selected' for a free federal grant — for bills, home repairs, or personal expenses — and only need to pay a processing or insurance fee to receive it. Real government grants require formal applications for specific programs and are never handed out by phone with a fee. The grant does not exist.
whatToDo: Real grants are listed at grants.gov and require applications — no fees by gift card.
Never pay to receive 'free' government money.
Ask for the program name and verify it on grants.gov.
Report the call to the FTC.

scams.example: U.S. Passport Services Online: Renew your passport in as little as 24 hours! Complete your application and pay the $189 expediting fee here. Official government forms included — avoid delays and travel disruptions, start now: us-passport-renewfast.com
scams.name: Fake Passport Service Scam
redFlags: Passport renewal offered in 24 hours for a big fee
Charges for government forms that are free
Site name mimics an official government service
Asks for SSN and card details on a non-.gov site
No real connection to the State Department
scams.summary: Websites and ads pose as official passport or visa services, charging high fees to 'expedite' your application or sell forms that are free from the government. Some simply steal your personal information and card number. The only official U.S. passport site is travel.state.gov.
whatToDo: Use only travel.state.gov for passport applications and renewals.
Download forms free from the official site.
Pay government fees only as instructed on the .gov site.
Report fake sites to the FTC.

scams.example: U.S. Department of State Notification: Congratulations, your entry was selected in the Diversity Visa Lottery. To proceed with your green card processing, submit the $430 visa issuance fee within 14 days using the payment instructions below.
scams.name: Diversity Visa Lottery Scam
redFlags: Claims you won the visa lottery by email
Fee demanded to claim or process the visa
Payment by wire, gift card, or crypto requested
No way to check status on the official dvprogram.state.gov site
Urgent deadline to keep your 'win' from expiring
scams.summary: An email or site announces that you 'won' the U.S. Diversity Visa (green card) lottery and must pay a fee to claim your visa. The real Diversity Visa program is free to enter, winners check their own status on the State Department website, and no payment is ever collected by email. Any payment demand proves it is fake.
whatToDo: Enter and check results only at dvprogram.state.gov — entry is free.
Winners are never notified by email asking for payment.
Never wire money for a visa lottery 'win.'
Report the message to the FTC and the State Department fraud unit.

scams.example: Reminder: Your driver's license expires this month. Renew online in minutes to avoid late penalties and keep your license valid. Have your license number and payment card ready: renew-license-online.com
scams.name: Fake License Renewal Site
redFlags: Renewal link sent by text or unsolicited email
Site asks for full SSN in addition to license details
Web address is not your state's official DMV domain
Promises to skip lines or tests for an extra fee
Payment page asks for card details before showing any official state branding
scams.summary: A text or email says your driver's license is expiring and directs you to renew online at a professional-looking copy of a DMV website. The fake site takes your renewal fee plus your license number, SSN, and card details for identity theft. Renew only through your state's official DMV site.
whatToDo: Type your state DMV's official website address yourself.
Check your actual license expiration date on the card itself.
Never renew through a link in a text message.
If you paid, call your bank and report the site to the FTC.

scams.example: Vehicle Registration Notice: Your registration renewal is now due. Complete your renewal online today to avoid a lapse in coverage and late fees. Plate and VIN verification required: state-vehicle-renewal.com
scams.name: Fake Vehicle Registration Renewal
redFlags: Renewal notice with a payment link from an unknown sender
Fees higher than your last renewal
Asks for VIN, plate, and SSN together
Site is not an official state or county domain
Notice arrives when your registration is not actually due
scams.summary: A notice by text, email, or mail says your vehicle registration is due and sends you to a fake renewal site that charges inflated fees — or harvests your plate, VIN, and card information. Some victims receive nothing at all. Legitimate renewals go through your state or county's official site or tax collector.
whatToDo: Check your registration's real expiration date on the decal or card.
Renew only through your state DMV or county tax collector's official site.
Compare the fee to what you paid last time.
Report the site or message to the FTC.

scams.example: Elections Alert: Our records show you are NOT registered to vote at your current address. The deadline is almost here — confirm your registration in 2 minutes so your vote counts: check-voter-registration.com
scams.name: Voter Registration Phishing Text
redFlags: Claims you are not registered and pushes a link
Registration offered through a text message link
Page asks for full ID or SSN digits plus date of birth
Site is not your state or county elections website
Artificial deadline pressure
scams.summary: A text claims you are not registered to vote, or that your registration has a problem, and pushes you to a link to 'register now.' The page harvests your name, address, date of birth, and ID numbers — and in most states you cannot even register by text. Check your status only through your state or county elections office.
whatToDo: Check your registration at vote.gov, which links to your official state site.
Never enter ID details on a site reached from a text.
Contact your county Supervisor of Elections directly with questions.
Forward the text to 7726 (SPAM).

scams.example: FORECLOSURE NOTICE: Foreclosure proceedings have been initiated on your property. You may still save your home through our hardship relief program. Call the foreclosure relief line at 1-800-555-0119 within 5 business days and have your first relief payment ready.
scams.name: Fake Foreclosure Relief Scam
redFlags: Foreclosure notice from a company you do not recognize
Fees demanded to stop foreclosure or 'start relief'
Told not to contact your mortgage lender or a lawyer
Asked to sign over your deed or make payments to a third party
Guarantees to save your home
scams.summary: An official-looking letter or call says foreclosure has started on your home and urges you to call a 'relief' line or pay fees to stop it. The scammers charge for help you can get free, or worse, trick owners into signing over their deed. Real foreclosure help from HUD-approved counselors is free.
whatToDo: Call your mortgage servicer directly using the number on your statement.
Get free help from a HUD-approved housing counselor at 1-800-569-4287.
Never pay a company to negotiate with your lender for you.
Report the notice to the FTC and your state attorney general.

scams.example: Dear customer, you have received a Zelle payment of $2,000.00. Your account must be upgraded to a business account to accept it. Please refund $500 to verify and upgrade your account, then the full amount will be released.
scams.name: Fake Zelle Payment Email
redFlags: Zelle has no 'business upgrade' for receiving money
You are asked to send money to receive money
The email did not come from your own bank
Urgent tone and a deadline to act
Payment confirmation with no alert inside your real bank app
scams.summary: You get an email saying someone sent you money by Zelle, but your account is 'personal' and cannot receive it until you upgrade to a business account. To upgrade, you are told to send money back to the sender first. The incoming payment was never real, so anything you send is gone for good.
whatToDo: Open your bank app yourself and check whether any payment is really there
Never send money to 'unlock' or 'upgrade' an incoming payment
Call your bank at the number on the back of your card
Report the email at reportfraud.ftc.gov

scams.example: Venmo Alert: You received $750.00 from a business account. To accept payments over $500, call Venmo support at 1-844-555-0132 to verify your identity within 24 hours or the funds will be returned.
scams.name: Fake Venmo Payment and Support Scam
redFlags: A support phone number that is not inside the Venmo app
Payment from a stranger for something you did not sell
Being asked to send money back for an 'error'
Requests for your password or a texted code
Urgency about funds being returned or frozen
scams.summary: Scammers send fake Venmo payment notices and run fake 'Venmo support' numbers found through search ads. They claim a payment was sent in error, or that your account needs verification, then talk you into sending real money or handing over a login code. Real Venmo support never works this way.
whatToDo: Check the Venmo app directly — if the payment is not there, it is fake
Only contact support through the app itself
Never read a texted code to anyone
Block the sender and report the message in the app

scams.example: Cash App Giveaway Team: Congratulations! You were selected to flip your balance. Send $50 clearance fee to $CashAppRewards and receive $500 back within 10 minutes. Limited spots today only!
scams.name: Fake Cash App Support and Money Flip
redFlags: Anyone promising to multiply money you send them
A 'clearance fee' or 'unlock fee' before a payout
Support contacted through social media or a search ad
Requests for your PIN, sign-in code, or full card number
Giveaways that Cash App never announced in its own app
scams.summary: Two tricks use the Cash App name. Fake support agents in search ads and social posts ask for your PIN or sign-in code, then drain your balance. 'Money flip' promoters promise to turn $100 into $1,000 after you pay a small clearance fee — the fee is all they ever collect.
whatToDo: Never pay a fee to receive money — that is always the scam
Contact Cash App only through the app's support section
Never share your PIN or sign-in code with anyone
Report the account inside Cash App and to the FTC

scams.example: This is Card Services calling about your current credit card account. You are now eligible for a much lower interest rate. Press 1 now to speak with a representative before this offer expires today.
scams.name: Credit Card Interest Rate Robocall
redFlags: A robocall that never names your actual card company
'Press 1' to reach a live agent
A final-notice warning you have heard many times before
A fee charged to lower your rate
Requests for full card numbers and security codes
scams.summary: A recorded voice says you qualify to lower your credit card interest rate and tells you to press 1 before the offer expires. A live agent then asks for your card numbers and charges a fee of hundreds of dollars for something you could request free from your card company — and often does nothing at all.
whatToDo: Hang up — do not press any buttons
Call your card company at the number on the back of your card and ask about rates directly
Never pay a fee to lower an interest rate
Register your number at donotcall.gov and report the call

scams.example: We can settle your $28,000 in credit card debt for just $9,000! Stop paying your cards today and let our experts negotiate. Enroll now — a one-time enrollment fee of $995 starts your program.
scams.name: Debt Relief and Settlement Scam
redFlags: Guarantees to settle debts for a specific fraction
Fees charged before any debt is actually settled
Told to stop paying and stop talking to your creditors
Claims of a special government program
Pressure to sign up on the first call
scams.summary: These companies promise to settle your debts for pennies on the dollar if you stop paying your creditors and pay them a monthly fee instead. Charging fees before settling anything is illegal, and many people end up deeper in debt, sued by creditors, with ruined credit.
whatToDo: Never pay an upfront fee for debt relief — it is illegal
Talk to a nonprofit credit counselor through nfcc.org instead
Check any company with your state attorney general
Keep paying your creditors until you have verified help

scams.example: We can stop your foreclosure guaranteed! Do not contact your lender again — send your monthly payments to our office while we negotiate. A processing fee of $2,500 is due this week to save your home.
scams.name: Foreclosure Rescue Scam
redFlags: A guarantee they can stop foreclosure
Told to stop paying your lender or stop contacting them
Mortgage payments redirected to the helper
Large upfront fees for paperwork
Asked to sign over the deed 'temporarily'
scams.summary: Posing as foreclosure helpers, scammers charge big fees and tell you to stop paying your mortgage and send payments to them instead. They pocket the money, do little or nothing with your lender, and you can lose the house. Real foreclosure help from HUD counselors is free.
whatToDo: Never pay for foreclosure help — HUD counselors are free at 1-800-569-4287
Keep paying your real lender directly
Never sign over your deed to a rescue company
Call your loan servicer at the number on your statement

scams.example: Congratulations! You are approved for a $10,000 personal loan regardless of credit history. To release your funds today, pay the $350 loan insurance fee by Cash App. This offer expires tonight.
scams.name: Advance-Fee Loan Scam
redFlags: Guaranteed approval with no credit check
Any fee required before you receive loan money
Fees requested by gift card, wire, or payment app
No verifiable business address or lender license
Offer expires within hours
scams.summary: You are 'guaranteed approved' for a loan no matter your credit, but first you must pay an application, insurance, or security fee by gift card, wire, or payment app. A real lender never asks for money before giving you money — after you pay, no loan ever arrives.
whatToDo: Never pay money to get a loan
Check the lender's license with your state regulator
Apply through your own bank or credit union instead
Report the offer at reportfraud.ftc.gov

scams.example: I need you to process an urgent wire of $84,250 for a confidential acquisition. Use the attached instructions and confirm when done. Do not discuss this with anyone — I am in meetings all day. — Sent from my phone
scams.name: Fake CEO Wire Transfer Email
redFlags: Urgency plus secrecy in the same request
Wire instructions sent as an attachment or new account
'Do not discuss this with anyone'
Sender address is a lookalike of the real company domain
Request skips the normal approval process
scams.summary: An email that looks like it came from the company boss orders an employee to wire money for a secret deal, today, with no questions asked. The address is spoofed or lookalike, and the wire goes straight to the scammer. Businesses lose millions to this one trick.
whatToDo: Call the executive at a known number to confirm — never reply to the email
Follow your company's normal payment approval steps, no exceptions
Check the full sender address, not just the display name
Report it to your IT department and the FBI at ic3.gov

scams.example: I mailed your check for $2,450 instead of $450 — a payroll mistake. Please deposit it today and send the extra $2,000 back by Zelle so we can close the books. Thank you for your honesty!
scams.name: Fake Check Overpayment Scam
redFlags: A check for more than the agreed amount
Asked to send part of the money back or onward
Pressure to act the same day the check arrives
Overpayment blamed on a 'mistake' or 'payroll error'
You are asked to buy gift cards with the extra
scams.summary: A buyer, employer, or prize sponsor sends you a check for more than agreed and asks you to send the difference back or buy gift cards with it. Your bank shows the money at first, but the check is counterfeit — when it bounces days later, you owe the bank everything you sent.
whatToDo: Never send money from a check someone else gave you
Wait at least two weeks for a check to fully clear before spending it
Tell your bank you suspect the check is fake
Stop all contact with the sender and report it

scams.example: Our blockchain forensics team traced your stolen Bitcoin and can recover it within 72 hours. Pay the recovery fee of $1,200 to begin. Success rate 98% — funds are located and frozen now.
scams.name: Crypto Recovery Service Scam
redFlags: Promises or guarantees to recover cryptocurrency
Any upfront fee before 'recovery' begins
They contacted you first, often on social media
Claims your funds are 'located and frozen'
Requests for wallet seed phrases or remote access
scams.summary: After someone loses cryptocurrency to a scam, 'recovery experts' appear promising to trace and return it — for an upfront fee. They cannot recover crypto, and they know victims are desperate. The fee disappears, and sometimes they drain whatever wallet access you give them.
whatToDo: Understand that lost crypto is almost never recoverable
Never pay an upfront recovery fee
Never share a seed phrase with anyone, ever
Report the original theft to the FBI at ic3.gov

scams.example: This is the Federal Refund Department. Our records show you are owed a refund of $18,400 from a previous fraud case. Pay the legal processing fee of $620 today to release your compensation.
scams.name: Fake Scam-Refund Agency
redFlags: A refund you never applied for
Any fee needed to release a refund or settlement
Agency names that sound official but are slightly off
They know details about a scam you really fell for
Payment requested by gift card or wire
scams.summary: Scammers target people who already lost money once, posing as refund agencies, law firms, or even the FTC itself. They say your refund is ready — you just owe taxes, legal fees, or a processing charge first. There is no refund; it is the same criminals coming back for more.
whatToDo: Real government refunds never require a fee first
Verify any agency independently — never use their phone number
Contact the real FTC at 1-877-382-4357
Assume it is the original scammers returning and hang up

scams.example: I turned $500 into $14,000 this month trading forex and so can you. DM me 'READY' to join my signals group. My broker is giving new students a 100% deposit bonus this week only!
scams.name: Social Media Forex Mentor Scam
redFlags: Guaranteed or 'risk-free' trading profits
Luxury lifestyle photos as proof of success
An unregistered offshore broker you were told to use
Fees or taxes required before any withdrawal
Recruitment through DMs and group chats
scams.summary: Flashy social media 'mentors' show off rented cars and fake trading dashboards promising guaranteed forex profits. You deposit into an unregistered offshore broker they control, watch fake gains grow, then pay fee after fee to withdraw — and never get a dollar back.
whatToDo: Check any broker at the CFTC and NFA websites before depositing
Never invest through a link from social media
Treat guaranteed returns as proof of fraud
Start with your own bank's or a licensed US broker's education pages

scams.example: SURPRISE AIRDROP: Your wallet was selected! Connect at claim-airdrop.xyz within 6 hours to receive your free NFT. Support: if the claim fails, DM our mod your wallet address for manual review.
scams.name: Fake NFT Mint and Airdrop Scam
redFlags: A mint or airdrop announced only in DMs or replies
Countdown timers measured in hours
Sites that ask for your seed phrase — no real site ever does
'Support' or 'mods' who message you first
Links that do not match the project's real website
scams.summary: Fake mint announcements, surprise 'airdrop' tokens, and phony support helpers in Discord and X direct you to connect your wallet to a lookalike site. Signing the transaction does not buy anything — it gives the scammer permission to drain your wallet.
whatToDo: Never type a seed phrase into any website
Verify announcements on the project's official page you found yourself
Keep savings in a wallet you never connect to mint sites
Revoke unknown wallet permissions at revoke.cash

scams.example: Your account has been compromised. Withdraw $9,800 in cash, go to the Bitcoin ATM at the gas station, and stay on the phone with me. I will give you the wallet QR code to send it to the secure federal account.
scams.name: Crypto ATM Payment Scam
redFlags: Any instruction to use a Bitcoin or crypto ATM
Told to stay on the phone the whole time
A QR code provided by the caller for the deposit
Warnings not to tell the bank or store clerk the real reason
Threats of arrest or account seizure today
scams.summary: A caller pretending to be your bank, the sheriff, or a utility coaches you to withdraw cash and feed it into a Bitcoin ATM 'to protect your money' or pay a fine. Crypto ATM payments cannot be reversed, and no real agency or business will ever ask for one.
whatToDo: Hang up — no real bank, sheriff, or utility takes crypto ATM payments
Call the real organization at its published number
If you already paid, call police and the ATM company immediately — speed matters
Warn the store clerk if you see someone being coached at a crypto ATM

scams.example: Text from your carrier: 'Your phone number has been transferred to a new SIM card. If you did not request this change, call us right away.' An hour later your phone shows No Service - and password reset emails you never asked for start arriving.
scams.name: SIM Swap Phone Takeover
redFlags: Your phone loses service suddenly with no explanation
Password reset texts or emails you did not request
Carrier emails about a SIM or number change you did not make
Being locked out of email or bank accounts right after
2FA codes arriving that you never asked for
signatures: has been transferred to a new sim
scams.summary: A scammer convinces your phone carrier to move your number to their SIM card using stolen personal details. Your phone goes dead while they receive your calls and texted login codes, then reset your email and bank passwords and drain accounts within the hour.
whatToDo: Call your carrier immediately from another phone and freeze your number
Ask your carrier to add a port-out PIN and account lock
Call your bank's fraud line and freeze accounts
Change passwords from a clean device, starting with email

scams.example: What you see: a slightly crooked sticker on the parking meter that says 'Scan to Pay — Fast & Easy!' The code opens parkpay-quick.com instead of the city's real parking app.
scams.name: Fake QR Code Sticker Scam
redFlags: A QR sticker that looks placed over another code
The payment page address is not the city's or restaurant's real site
The page asks for full card details for a tiny fee
No option to pay at the meter itself
Emails later showing charges you do not recognize
scams.summary: Scammers stick their own QR codes over real ones on parking meters, restaurant tables, and vending machines. Scanning takes you to a convincing fake payment page that steals your card details — and you still owe the real parking fee or get a ticket.
whatToDo: Peel-check any QR code — if it is a sticker on a sticker, do not scan
Type the official app or website name yourself instead
Pay at the meter or front desk when you can
Report the fake code to the business and your card issuer if you paid

scams.example: You scratch a gift card you were just given and check the balance: $0.00 - already spent online this morning, before the card was even handed to you. The number was copied off the rack in the store days earlier.
scams.name: Drained Gift Card Scam
redFlags: Scratch-off PIN area that looks re-covered or tampered with
Packaging that is bent, re-glued, or different from neighbors
A zero balance the first time the recipient checks
Cards taken from the very front of the rack
Store cannot see the balance being spent elsewhere
scams.summary: Thieves record the numbers off gift cards hanging in store racks, then wait for the card to be bought and loaded. They drain the balance within hours — sometimes before the gift is even opened. The giver did nothing wrong; the card was copied in the store.
whatToDo: Pick cards from the middle or back of the rack and inspect the PIN cover
Give the receipt with the card so the balance can be proven
Have the recipient check the balance right away
Report a drained card to the issuer and store immediately — quick reports sometimes get restored

scams.example: You and a guest are invited to a FREE gourmet dinner seminar: 'How to Retire Tax-Free and Never Outlive Your Money.' Seating is limited — reserve today. Attendees receive a complimentary retirement blueprint.
scams.name: Free Dinner Investment Seminar Scam
redFlags: Free meals used to sell financial products
Fear stories about market crashes and running out of money
Bonuses for signing before you leave
Products you cannot easily compare or cancel
Advisors who will not put promises in writing
scams.summary: A glossy invitation offers a free steak dinner and 'retirement education.' The seminar is a sales trap for high-commission products — pricey annuities, timeshares, or 'can't-lose' schemes — sold with fear stories and sign-today pressure aimed at retirees.
whatToDo: Enjoy the dinner if you like — but never sign anything there
Take materials home and check the seller at brokercheck.finra.org
Ask what the product costs per year, in dollars, in writing
Get a second opinion from a fiduciary advisor you chose yourself

scams.example: WARNING: The coming bank collapse will wipe out paper IRAs. Protect yourself — roll over to a Gold IRA today. Act now and receive $10,000 in FREE silver on qualifying accounts. Call our senior specialists.
scams.name: Gold IRA Rollover Scam
redFlags: Collapse and confiscation scare stories
'Free silver' offers worth thousands of dollars
Pressure to move your entire retirement account
Coin prices never compared to the plain metal price
Sellers who are not licensed investment advisors
scams.summary: Fear-based ads warn that banks and the dollar are about to collapse, then push you to roll your IRA into 'physical gold' coins sold at markups of 100% or more. The coins are real but wildly overpriced, and your retirement savings shrink the day you buy.
whatToDo: Compare any coin price to the day's spot gold price before buying
Never roll over an IRA on a cold call
Ask for the full markup and buyback policy in writing
Talk to your current IRA custodian or a fiduciary first

scams.example: Be your own boss! Join our team for a $499 starter kit and earn $5,000 a month from home. The products sell themselves — your real income comes from building your team. Bring two friends to tonight's Zoom!
scams.name: Pyramid Scheme 'Business Opportunity'
redFlags: Income claims based on recruiting other people
A starter kit or inventory you must buy to qualify
Earnings screenshots instead of real sales records
Meetings built on hype, not product details
Most participants quietly lose money
scams.summary: Recruiters sell a dream of easy income, but the money comes from signing up new recruits — and buying starter kits and inventory — not from real customers. Nearly everyone at the bottom loses money while the top few collect. If the pitch is about recruiting, it is a pyramid, not a business.
whatToDo: Ask what share of income comes from sales to real customers
Read the company's income disclosure statement before paying anything
Never buy inventory to 'qualify' for commissions
Search the company name plus 'complaints' and check ftc.gov

scams.example: Hello, due to a banking change, please use the UPDATED wiring instructions attached for your closing funds of $87,400. Send by Thursday to avoid delaying closing. — Escrow Department, First Title Group
scams.name: Home Closing Wire Fraud
redFlags: Wire instructions changed at the last minute
The change arrives only by email
A new bank or account name you have not seen before
Pressure about closing being delayed
Sender domain off by one letter from the real company
scams.summary: Days before closing on a home, the buyer gets an email that looks like the title company or realtor with 'updated' wire instructions. The new account belongs to a scammer. Once a closing wire is sent, it is usually gone within hours and the sale collapses.
whatToDo: Call the title company at a number you already had — never one from the email
Confirm account details in person or by a known voice before wiring
Set a verbal password with your title company at the start
If a bad wire went out, call your bank and the FBI (ic3.gov) within the hour

scams.example: We GUARANTEE a 750 credit score in 45 days! We delete bankruptcies, late payments, even repossessions. Plus tradelines for sale — get added as an authorized user and boost your score instantly. Setup fee $1,499.
scams.name: Credit Repair Scam
redFlags: Guaranteed score increases or deletion of true information
Upfront fees — illegal for credit repair companies
'Tradelines for sale' or paid authorized-user offers
Told to dispute everything, even accurate items
Asked to use a CPN instead of your Social Security number
scams.summary: These companies promise to erase bankruptcies, late payments, and bad scores — sometimes by adding you as an 'authorized user' on a stranger's card for a fee. They cannot legally remove accurate information, charging upfront is illegal, and paid tradelines can get your applications flagged as fraud.
whatToDo: Never pay upfront for credit repair — it is illegal to charge you
Get free reports at annualcreditreport.com and dispute errors yourself for free
Never buy authorized-user tradelines or a CPN
Rebuild credit with a secured card from your own bank

scams.example: What arrives: an IRS letter saying a 2025 return was already filed under your Social Security number — or your e-filed return is rejected as a 'duplicate filing' when you know you never filed.
scams.name: Tax Refund Identity Theft
redFlags: Your return is rejected as already filed
An IRS letter about a return you did not submit
A tax transcript or refund you never requested
Wages reported from an employer you never worked for
IRS notices about online accounts you did not create
scams.summary: A thief with your Social Security number files a fake tax return early in the season claiming a refund to their account. You find out months later when the IRS rejects your real return or sends a letter about a return you never filed. Prevention is much easier than the cleanup.
whatToDo: File IRS Form 14039 (Identity Theft Affidavit) right away
Get a free IRS Identity Protection PIN at irs.gov for future filings
Respond to IRS letters by mail using the number printed on the notice
Place a free credit freeze with all three bureaus

scams.example: This is Investigator Collins from your bank's fraud unit. Your branch staff are under investigation and your savings are at risk tonight. Transfer everything to the safe account I give you, and do not tell the branch why.
scams.name: Fake 'Safe Account' Bank Investigator Scam
redFlags: Any instruction to move money to a 'safe account'
Claims that bank employees themselves are the thieves
Orders not to tell branch staff or family
Caller asks you to lie to your bank about the reason
Transfers directed to an account in someone else's name
scams.summary: A caller claiming to be a bank investigator or police officer says your money is about to be stolen by criminals or dishonest bank staff, so you must move it to a 'safe account' they provide. That account is the scammer's. Real banks never move your money this way.
whatToDo: Hang up — banks never ask customers to move money for an investigation
Go into your branch or call the number on your statement
Tell the teller the full real story; staff are trained to spot this
Report the call to your bank and the FTC

scams.example: Important: Following our merger, all online banking customers must confirm their details by Friday to avoid losing access. Log in securely at first-community-verify.com and re-enter your username, password, and debit card number.
scams.name: Fake Bank Merger Notice Scam
redFlags: A merger you cannot find in real news or on your bank's real site
A login link inside the notice
Asked to re-enter full card numbers or Social Security number
Access-loss deadlines measured in days
Website address that is close to, but not exactly, your bank's
scams.summary: An email or letter announces your bank has merged or been bought, and you must 'confirm your details' on a new website to keep online access. The site is a lookalike that harvests your username, password, and card details. Real merger notices never ask you to log in from a link.
whatToDo: Type your bank's web address yourself or use its app — never the link
Call the number on your statement to ask about any merger
Remember: real banks never ask for full card details by email
Report the site at reportfraud.ftc.gov

scams.example: Beautiful 3BR house, $850/mo, all utilities included! I am out of state for work so I cannot show it, but you can drive by. First month free if you wire the $600 deposit today to hold it - many people are asking about this one.
scams.name: Fake Landlord Rental Scam
redFlags: Rent is far below other homes in the same area
Landlord cannot meet in person or show the home
Deposit must be wired, sent by app, or paid in gift cards
Pressure to pay today before someone else gets it
Photos look copied from a real estate website
signatures: first month free if you wire
god bless, i am a missionary
rent to own, bad credit ok
scams.summary: The scammer copies photos from a real home listing and reposts them with rent that is suspiciously low. The 'landlord' says he is out of town and asks you to wire a deposit to hold the home before you ever see it. There is no home to rent - the deposit is gone and the 'landlord' disappears.
whatToDo: Never wire money for a home you have not been inside
Search the address online - the home may be listed for sale or rented by someone else for much more
Meet the landlord in person and ask to see proof they own the property
Report the ad to the website where you found it
