scams.example: We can move your whole house for just $899, best price guaranteed! (On moving day:) The load is heavier than estimated, so the total is now $3,400. We need cash before we can unload - no checks, no cards.
scams.name: Moving Company Hostage Scam
redFlags: Quote given over the phone without seeing your belongings
Price is far lower than other movers
No written contract, or the contract is mostly blank
Price jumps after your things are loaded
Cash-only payment demanded before unloading
signatures: sign here, we will fill in
scams.summary: A mover gives you a very low quote over the phone, much cheaper than everyone else. On moving day, after your belongings are loaded on the truck, the price suddenly jumps by thousands. They refuse to unload your things until you pay the new amount in cash.
whatToDo: Get in-home or video estimates from at least three movers, in writing
Check the company's license number on the federal mover database (FMCSA)
If your goods are held hostage, call the police non-emergency line and the FMCSA complaint line
Never sign a blank or incomplete contract

scams.example: Hi ma'am, we're doing roofs on your street and I noticed loose shingles on yours. We have leftover materials from a job nearby, so I can do it today for $1,800 - I just need $900 cash today to get started.
scams.name: Door-to-Door Home Repair Scam
redFlags: Knocked on your door uninvited offering repairs
'Leftover materials' or a one-day-only price
Cash deposit demanded before work starts
No business card, license number, or written contract
Truck has no company name or has out-of-state plates
signatures: insurance will cover it, sign here
don't tell your neighbors this price
scams.summary: A friendly 'contractor' knocks on your door saying he noticed damage to your roof, driveway, or trees - often right after a storm. He offers a great price if you pay a cash deposit today, then does sloppy work or vanishes with the money. Sometimes the 'repair' is just black paint sprayed on a roof or driveway.
whatToDo: Never hire anyone who knocks on your door the same day
Ask for a license number and check it with your state before paying anything
Get two more written quotes from local companies
Pay by check or card made out to the business, never cash to a person

scams.example: Great news - your home qualifies for the free solar program! Your electric bill goes to $0 and there is no cost to you. I just need you to sign on my tablet today before the program fills up in your area.
scams.name: Free Solar Panel Scam
redFlags: Claims panels are free through a government program
Promises your electric bill will be zero
Sign today - the program is 'filling up'
Contract signed on a tablet without time to read it
No mention of a lease, loan, or payments that rise yearly
scams.summary: Salespeople promise 'free solar panels' from a government program and an electric bill of zero. In reality you may be signing a 25-year lease or loan with payments that go up every year. Some contracts put a lien on your home and make it hard to sell.
whatToDo: Never sign anything the same day it is offered
Ask directly: is this a loan or a lease, what is the total cost, and does it rise?
Read the full contract at home and check for a lien on your house
Get quotes from two other solar companies and call your power company about real rates

scams.example: FINAL NOTICE: Our records show your home warranty coverage is about to expire. Failure to renew may leave you responsible for all repair costs. Call 1-800-555-0146 within 5 days to keep your property protected.
scams.name: Home Warranty Letter Scam
redFlags: Urgent 'final notice' about a warranty you never bought
Letter looks official but has no real company name you recognize
Claims your lender requires the warranty (it does not)
Phone call demands bank or card details right away
Vague promises - the fine print excludes most repairs
signatures: your coverage is about to expire
scams.summary: You get an official-looking letter saying your home warranty is expiring or that a warranty is 'required' with your mortgage. It is really a sales pitch for an expensive plan that covers very little. Some letters pretend to be from your lender so you call and hand over bank details.
whatToDo: Check with your actual mortgage lender before believing the letter
Search the company name plus the word 'complaints' before calling
Never give bank details to an unsolicited caller
If you already paid, call your bank and ask about disputing the charge

scams.example: We guarantee we can exit your timeshare contract within 180 days, guaranteed, or your money back! We have a buyer waiting in your area. All we need is a $4,500 processing fee today to start the paperwork.
scams.name: Timeshare Exit Scam
redFlags: Big up-front fee before any work is done
'Money-back guarantee' from a company you have never heard of
Claims a buyer is already waiting for your timeshare
Pressures you at a dinner or hotel presentation
Advises you to stop paying your timeshare fees (this harms your credit)
signatures: we will get you out in 180 days
we have a buyer waiting in your area
processing fee today to start the paperwork
scams.summary: A company promises it can legally cancel your timeshare or even sell it for a profit - for a fee of thousands of dollars paid up front. Most victims pay and hear nothing more; their timeshare, and its yearly fees, are still theirs. Some are talked into buying a second timeshare to 'trade up.'
whatToDo: Never pay an exit company up front - legitimate help is rare and never rushed
Call your resort directly; some take units back for free
Search the company with the Better Business Bureau and your state attorney general
If you paid by card, dispute the charge with your bank right away

scams.example: Oceanfront condo, sleeps 8, only $99/night for July 4th week! Book direct with me and skip the site fees - just send half by Venmo to hold your dates, it books up fast.
scams.name: Fake Vacation Rental Scam
redFlags: Price is far below similar rentals in the area
Owner wants payment outside the booking platform
Owner asks for payment by Venmo, Zelle, Cash App, or wire
Cannot video-call you from inside the property
Listing photos also appear under a different address
signatures: book direct and skip the fees
send half to hold your dates
pay outside the app for a discount
by venmo to hold your dates
scams.summary: A beautiful beach condo or cabin is advertised on social media or a marketplace at a great price, using stolen photos. The 'owner' asks you to pay by Venmo, Zelle, or wire to get a deal outside the booking site. When you arrive, the home belongs to someone else - or does not exist at all.
whatToDo: Only book and pay through a known rental platform
Search the property address and a few of the listing's words to find the real listing
Ask for a live video walk-through before paying anything
Pay by credit card so you can dispute the charge if it is fake

scams.example: Congratulations! You've been selected to earn $400/week just by driving with our energy drink decal on your car. We've mailed your first check of $3,850 - keep $400 and send the rest to our certified wrap installer to book your appointment.
scams.name: Car Wrap Advertising Scam
redFlags: Easy money for doing almost nothing
A check arrives for much more than your pay
You are told to forward money to an 'installer' or 'agent'
Payment must be sent fast, by wire or gift cards
Everything handled by text or email - no real company office
signatures: paid to drive your own car
scams.summary: You are offered $400 a week to put an advertising wrap on your car for a drink or snack brand. They mail you a check for more than your first payment and tell you to send the extra money to the 'installer.' The check is fake - it bounces after your real money is already gone.
whatToDo: Never deposit a check and send part of the money on to someone else
Wait at least two weeks for any check to fully clear before spending it
Contact the real brand through its official website and ask if the program exists
Report the offer to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov

scams.example: Your first assignment: visit the store near you, purchase $2,000 in gift cards as part of our quality evaluation, and send us photos of the card numbers. Your check for $2,450 (including your $450 pay) is enclosed.
scams.name: Mystery Shopper Scam
redFlags: Hired with no interview, application, or experience
A check arrives before you do any work
Job involves buying gift cards and reporting the numbers
You must complete the task the same day
They discourage you from telling the store what you are doing
signatures: send photos of the card numbers
your pay is included in the check
send us photos of the card numbers
scams.summary: You are 'hired' as a mystery shopper and sent a check to cover your purchases and pay. The assignment: buy gift cards or money orders and report the numbers right away. Days later the check bounces, the gift cards are emptied, and you owe the bank the full amount.
whatToDo: Never use a new employer's check to buy gift cards for them
Real mystery shopper jobs pay small amounts AFTER the work, by payroll
Ask your bank to verify the check before depositing it
Report the offer to the FTC and throw the check away

scams.example: CLEARANCE EVENT - up to 90% OFF! Premium stand mixer, was $549, now $54.99. Selling fast - only 7 left! Order now at kitchen-deals-outlet.example and pay with your card today.
scams.name: Fake Online Store Scam
redFlags: Prices are 70-90% off famous brand names
Store you have never heard of, found only through an ad
'Only a few left' countdowns and pressure to buy now
No real address, phone number, or returns page
Store name in the web address does not match a real retailer
scams.summary: Ads on social media show a slick store selling brand-name goods at impossible prices - a $600 grill for $59, designer shoes for $25. You pay, and either nothing arrives, a cheap knockoff arrives, or your card details are stolen and used for other charges.
whatToDo: Search the store name plus 'scam' or 'reviews' before ordering
Buy brand-name goods from the brand's own site or a store you know
Pay with a credit card, never a debit card, on new websites
If nothing arrives, dispute the charge with your card company

scams.example: Try our anti-aging cream FREE! Just pay $4.95 shipping. (In tiny print: after 14 days your card is charged $89.95 every month until you call a number that is almost never answered.)
scams.name: Free Trial Subscription Trap
redFlags: 'Free' product that still needs your card number
You only pay shipping - the catch is in the fine print
No clear price shown for after the trial
Cancellation only by calling a hard-to-reach phone number
Charges on your statement under a name you do not know
signatures: your card will be charged after
as seen on tv, free bottle
after 14 days your card is charged
scams.summary: An offer promises a free or $1 trial of a cream, supplement, or app - you only pay small shipping. Hidden in fine print, the trial starts an expensive monthly subscription that is nearly impossible to cancel. Small charges appear under names you do not recognize.
whatToDo: Read every word of the terms before entering card details for any 'free' trial
Set a calendar reminder before the trial ends and cancel in writing
Call your card company and dispute charges you did not agree to
Ask your bank to block the merchant if charges keep coming

scams.example: Fans are stunned! She lost 32 lbs in one month with these keto gummies - no diet needed! Get your FREE bottle today, just cover $6.95 shipping before this offer ends tonight.
scams.name: Celebrity Weight Loss Trial Scam
redFlags: A celebrity or TV doctor 'endorses' a miracle product
Huge weight loss promised with no effort
Free bottle - you only pay shipping
Offer 'ends tonight' or stock is almost gone
The story looks like a news article but is really an ad
scams.summary: Fake stories claim a TV doctor or celebrity lost weight with miracle gummies or drops, and offer a 'free bottle.' It is really a subscription: about $90 a month in charges that are very hard to stop. The celebrity never endorsed the product - their photo was stolen.
whatToDo: Check the celebrity's real social media - they did not post this
Never give card details for a 'free' bottle
Talk to your own doctor before trying any weight-loss product
Dispute the charges with your card company and ask them to block the seller

scams.example: Notice: You were overcharged $128.40 on your last order. We apologize for the error. Claim your refund within 24 hours by confirming your card details at support-refund-center.example.
scams.name: Overcharge Refund Scam
redFlags: Claims an overcharge you do not recognize
Refund requires your full card or bank login on a website
Link in the message goes to a look-alike website
Refund expires in 24 hours unless you act
Real refunds never need your Social Security number
scams.summary: A text or email claims a store or service charged you twice, and a refund is waiting. The 'refund form' asks for your full card number, bank login, or Social Security number. There was no overcharge - the form itself is the theft.
whatToDo: Do not use the link in the message
Check your account by opening the company's real app or website yourself
Call the number on the back of your card and ask if any refund is real
Delete the message - real companies refund automatically to your original payment

scams.example: 2019 SUV, only 40k miles, $4,200 firm - must sell fast, I am being deployed overseas. The car is already with SafeAuto Shippers; just wire the payment to their escrow account and they will deliver it to you in 3 days with a money-back guarantee.
scams.name: Too-Cheap Car Buying Scam
redFlags: Price is thousands below what the car is worth
Seller has an urgent story and cannot meet in person
Car is 'already with a shipping company'
Payment must be wired to an escrow or shipping account
Seller will not let you inspect the car or see the title
signatures: deliver it to you in 3 days
wire the payment to their escrow account
scams.summary: A car is listed far below its value, often with a sad story - a soldier deploying, a divorce, a death in the family. The seller says a shipping or 'escrow' company will deliver the car safely after you wire the money. The escrow company is fake too, and there is no car.
whatToDo: Never wire money for a car you have not seen and driven
Insist on meeting at the seller's home or a police station safe-exchange zone
Check the VIN online and see the title in person before paying
Search the listing text and photos - scammers reuse them in many cities

scams.example: This is your final courtesy call. Our records show your vehicle's factory warranty has expired or is about to expire. Press 1 now to speak with a warranty specialist and protect your vehicle from costly repairs.
scams.name: Auto Warranty Robocall Scam
redFlags: Robocall about a warranty you may not even have
'Final notice' pressure to act right now
Caller will not name your car's make, model, or dealer
Contract must be bought today with a card over the phone
The company name keeps changing between calls
signatures: press 1 to speak with a specialist
protect your vehicle from costly repairs
this is your last chance to renew
coverage for your vehicle is ending
scams.summary: Robocalls and letters warn that your car's warranty is about to expire and urge you to buy a service contract before it is 'too late.' The contracts are expensive, cover very little, and are almost impossible to cancel. The caller is not your car maker or dealer - they bought your information.
whatToDo: Hang up - your car maker does not sell warranties by robocall
Call your dealer or check your car's paperwork for real warranty dates
Never pay for a service contract over the phone the same day
Register your number on the Do Not Call list at donotcall.gov

scams.example: Two floor seats for Saturday's sold-out show, face value! I can't go anymore. Pay by Cash App and I'll transfer the tickets right away - screenshots of the mobile tickets attached so you know they're real.
scams.name: Fake Concert Ticket Scam
redFlags: Sold-out event tickets offered at or below face value
Seller wants Cash App, Venmo, or Zelle instead of a resale platform
Ticket proof is just a screenshot of a barcode
Seller rushes you because 'someone else is about to buy'
Brand-new or almost empty social media profile
signatures: someone else is about to buy
sold out show, my loss your gain
scams.summary: Scammers sell tickets to sold-out concerts and games through social media posts and fake resale sites. The 'tickets' are screenshots of barcodes, copies sold to many people, or simply made up. At the gate, the scan fails and your money is gone.
whatToDo: Buy only through the venue or a resale site with a buyer guarantee
Never pay a stranger by Cash App, Venmo, or Zelle for tickets
Remember a screenshot is not a ticket - real mobile tickets transfer inside the app
If the price looks too good for a sold-out show, it is fake

scams.example: I found your dog, he's fine but I need the $200 reward before I bring him. Also, to prove you're the real owner, I'll send you a code - just read the numbers back to me and then we can meet.
scams.name: Lost Pet Scam
redFlags: Caller will not send a photo of your pet
Demands gift cards, wire, or payment before meeting
Asks you to read back a verification code sent to your phone
Claims your pet is injured and needs vet money wired fast
Caller gets details wrong that only the real finder would know
signatures: read the code back to me
he's at the vet, send money
send a gift card for the reward
i have your cat, pay first
scams.summary: When your pet goes missing, you post flyers and ads with your phone number. A scammer calls claiming to have found your pet - sometimes saying it is hurt at a vet - and demands a reward, gift cards, or a code sent to your phone before they will meet you. They never had your pet.
whatToDo: Ask for a photo of your pet before discussing any reward
Never read back a code - that code is meant to hijack your accounts
Agree to meet at a police station or animal shelter, and pay only when your pet is in your arms
Keep one detail about your pet out of your ads to test anyone who calls

scams.example: Hello, I'm calling for the National Children's Cancer Relief Fund. Children in your state are counting on you today. Can I put you down for $75? I can take your card right now, it only takes a moment.
scams.name: Fake Charity Scam
redFlags: Charity name sounds like a famous one but is slightly different
High-pressure ask to donate right now, by phone
Caller cannot say how much of your gift helps the cause
Asks for gift cards, wire, or cash instead of a check or card
Thanks you for a donation you never made ('your pledge last year')
signatures: can i put you down for
children in your state are counting on you
every dollar goes to the families
we are calling all your neighbors
will you help the kids today
scams.summary: Callers and messages ask for donations to charities with names that sound almost exactly like famous real ones. The money goes to the scammer, or to a group that spends nearly everything on itself. They push hard for payment on the spot, especially right after sad news stories.
whatToDo: Never donate on a surprise phone call - hang up and research first
Check the charity at charitynavigator.org or your state's charity registry
Donate through the charity's own website, spelled carefully by you
Ask what percentage of donations goes to the cause - real charities answer clearly

scams.example: URGENT: Hurricane victims in our state need you NOW. Our Florida Storm Relief Fund is matching every gift today. Text DONATE or send gift cards - families have lost everything and help can't wait.
scams.name: Disaster Donation Scam
redFlags: Brand-new relief fund created right after the disaster
Emotional pressure to give immediately, today only
Asks for gift cards, crypto, or payment apps
Fund name copies a real agency but is not the real one
No way to verify the group existed before the disaster
scams.summary: Within hours of a hurricane, fire, or flood, fake relief appeals flood social media and text messages. They copy real photos of the damage and use names that sound like official relief funds. Donations go to the scammer while real victims get nothing.
whatToDo: Give to relief groups you already know, through their official websites
Be suspicious of any fund created after the disaster date
Search the fund's name plus 'scam' before donating
Never donate by gift card - no real charity accepts them

scams.example: Please help baby Emma's family after the terrible accident - funeral costs and medical bills are crushing them. Every share and dollar helps. Donate here: give-support-emma.example (page uses the family's real photos, copied from the news).
scams.name: Fake Fundraiser Scam
redFlags: Fundraiser organizer is not a family member you can verify
Page copies photos and text from news stories
Several similar pages exist for the same victim
Organizer pressures sharing before the family confirms it
Funds go to a personal account, not the family or a funeral home
signatures: goal is almost reached, give today
scams.summary: After a tragedy makes the news, scammers copy the victim's photos and story into their own fundraiser pages on crowdfunding sites and social media. Money meant for a grieving family goes to a stranger's account instead. Some fake pages appear before the real family has set anything up.
whatToDo: Check the family's or funeral home's official page for the one real fundraiser link
Donate only through the fundraiser the family has publicly confirmed
Report copycat pages to the crowdfunding site
When in doubt, give to a local charity helping with the disaster instead

scams.example: Hello, this is the American Veterans Support Foundation calling. Our brave heroes are suffering and your neighbors have all given $50. Can our veterans count on you for the same today? I'll just need your card number.
scams.name: Fake Veterans Charity Scam
redFlags: Official-sounding name you have never heard of
Caller says your neighbors have all donated
A large share of money goes to telemarketers, not veterans
Pressure to give on this call, by card
They call repeatedly, even after you ask them to stop
signatures: can our veterans count on you
scams.summary: Persistent callers ask for donations to help veterans, police, or firefighters, often with official-sounding names. Many of these groups are 'sound-alike' outfits that keep almost every dollar for their paid telemarketers. Your gift does little or nothing for the people in the ads.
whatToDo: Hang up and look the group up at charitynavigator.org before giving a cent
Well-known veterans groups can be reached through their own websites
Ask your state attorney general's office about the group's record
Consider giving to a local veterans post or shelter you can visit

scams.example: Your streaming membership is ON HOLD: we could not process your last payment. Update your billing within 48 hours to keep watching: streamflix-account-verify.example/signin
scams.name: Streaming Account Hold Scam
redFlags: Account 'on hold' threat with a deadline
Link goes to a website that is not the real service's name
Page asks for card number and password together
Message arrives even though your last payment went through
Sender email or number is not the company you pay
signatures: we could not process your payment
could not process your last payment
scams.summary: A text or email says your streaming account is on hold because a payment failed, with a link to 'update your payment.' The link leads to a perfect copy of the real sign-in page. Anything you type - password and card number - goes straight to the scammer.
whatToDo: Never use a link from the message - open the app or type the real website yourself
Check your account status after signing in the normal way
If you entered your password, change it right away and anywhere you reused it
Turn on two-step sign-in so a stolen password alone is not enough

scams.example: Good news from your TV provider! You've been selected for our loyalty promotion - 50% off for 12 months. Just prepay the first 3 months using eBay gift cards, $150 total, and the discount starts today.
scams.name: Half-Price Cable Scam
redFlags: Huge discount offered on an unsolicited call
Must prepay months in advance to get the deal
Payment demanded in gift cards or a payment app
Caller says the offer expires today
Your real provider's name is used but the callback number is different
signatures: gift cards to activate the offer
scams.summary: A caller claiming to be from your cable or satellite company offers half price for a year - if you prepay several months up front using gift cards or a payment app. Real TV companies never take gift cards. Your bill never changes, and the 'promotion' money is gone.
whatToDo: Hang up and call your provider at the number on your real bill
Remember: no real cable or phone company accepts gift cards as payment
Never prepay for a promotion you cannot see in writing on your account
Report the call to the FTC and your provider's fraud department

scams.example: LOYAL CUSTOMER ALERT: You've earned a FREE phone upgrade! Claim yours before midnight at mycarrier-upgrade-claim.example - just sign in with your account to confirm your shipping address.
scams.name: Fake Carrier Upgrade Scam
redFlags: Free upgrade you never applied for
Deadline of hours - 'before midnight'
Link is not your carrier's real website name
Page asks for your account password and PIN
Text comes from a random number, not your carrier's usual short code
signatures: sign in to confirm your address
confirm shipping to receive your phone
scams.summary: A text from your 'phone carrier' says you have earned a free phone upgrade or loyalty gift, with a link to claim it. The site looks exactly like your carrier's but is a copy built to steal your account login. With your login, scammers can order phones charged to your account.
whatToDo: Open your carrier's real app or website yourself to check for real offers
Call your carrier at the number on your bill if you are unsure
Never sign in to your phone account through a text link
If you signed in, change your password and PIN immediately

scams.example: Yes, we are the factory-authorized service. Our technician can come today - diagnostic is $289, and if we need the control board it's $650 paid today so we can order it. Most customers just do it while we're here.
scams.name: Fake Appliance Repair Scam
redFlags: Company found only through a search ad, name mimics a real brand
Diagnostic fee far higher than the usual $75-$125
Full payment for parts demanded before any work
Technician has no uniform, invoice, or business card
No written estimate or receipt with a real address
signatures: pay today so we can order the part
cash or zelle for the deposit
no receipt, it's in the system
scams.summary: You find a repair company online, often an ad at the top of search results, with a name close to a real brand's service department. The 'technician' charges a huge diagnostic fee, says a part must be ordered with full payment up front - and never comes back. The part was never ordered.
whatToDo: Call the manufacturer's real number from your appliance manual, not a search ad
Get the diagnosis and estimate in writing before paying anything
Pay by credit card, never cash, for repair work
Check reviews under the company's exact name and address before booking

scams.example: Your Apple ID has been locked for security reasons. A charge of $349.99 for iCloud storage is pending. Verify your account within 12 hours to avoid deletion: appleid-verify-secure.example.com
scams.name: Fake Apple ID Lockout
redFlags: Claims your Apple ID is locked or about to be deleted
A big charge you never made is mentioned to panic you
The link is not apple.com, no matter how close it looks
A deadline of just a few hours to act
Asks for your full card number and security code to 'verify'
signatures: your apple id has been locked
scams.summary: An email or text claims your Apple ID has been locked, or that you were charged hundreds of dollars for something you never bought. The link leads to a fake Apple page that steals your password and card details when you 'verify' your account. Apple never locks accounts this way or asks you to fix it through a link in a message.
whatToDo: Do not tap the link or call any number in the message
Check your account yourself by opening Settings on your iPhone or going to apple.com
Look at your real purchase history there — if the charge is not listed, the message was fake
Delete the message and report it as junk

scams.example: Hi, this is Facebook Support. A login code was sent to your phone by mistake. Please send us the 6-digit code so we can restore your friend's account before it is closed.
scams.name: Fake Facebook Recovery Scam
redFlags: A 'friend' asks for a code that was sent to your phone
Claims to be Facebook support contacting you by message or text
Urgency about an account being closed today
Real friends asking for codes through Messenger after being 'locked out'
Facebook support never contacts people this way
signatures: code was sent to your phone
i got locked out of my account
scams.summary: A message that looks like Facebook support — or a 'friend' whose account was already stolen — says you can help recover an account by sharing the login code just sent to your phone. That code is actually for YOUR account. Once you hand it over, the scammer takes over your page and uses it to scam your friends and family.
whatToDo: Never share a login code with anyone, for any reason
Call the friend on a number you already have and ask if it is really them
Turn on two-factor authentication in your Facebook settings
Report the message inside Facebook and block the sender

scams.example: Congratulations! Your account is eligible for a verified badge. Complete your application within 24 hours and pay the one-time $29 processing fee: instagram-badge-apply.example.com
scams.name: Instagram Verification Badge Scam
redFlags: Offers a verification badge through a message or email
Asks for a fee — real badges are not sold by message
The link is not instagram.com
A 24-hour deadline to claim the badge
Asks for your password outside the app
signatures: confirm your identity to get verified
scams.summary: You get a message saying your account qualifies for the blue verification badge — just apply or pay a small fee through a link. The page is fake and steals your login, and sometimes your card too. Real verification happens only inside the Instagram app, and Instagram never messages you about it.
whatToDo: Ignore the message — Instagram never offers badges this way
Only request verification inside the app under Settings, and it is free to apply
If you entered your password, change it right away in the app
Turn on two-factor authentication

scams.example: Hey, sorry — I accidentally sent my WhatsApp code to your number. It's a 6-digit code starting with 4. Can you screenshot it and send it to me quickly?
scams.name: WhatsApp Code Forwarding Scam
redFlags: Anyone asks you to forward or screenshot a code sent to you
The 'friend' cannot voice-call you to prove who they are
You just received a WhatsApp code you did not request
Pressure to send the code quickly
signatures: sent my code to your number
my code was sent to you
scams.summary: A message from a 'friend' says they accidentally sent their WhatsApp login code to your number and asks you to forward it. There is no accident — the code is the one WhatsApp sends to log in to YOUR account. Once the scammer has it, they lock you out and message all your contacts asking for money.
whatToDo: Never share a WhatsApp code with anyone, ever
Call the person on their regular number to check if it is really them
If you already sent a code, open WhatsApp and log back in immediately to kick them out
Set up a two-step verification PIN in WhatsApp settings

scams.example: Your mailbox has reached 98% of its storage limit. Incoming messages will be rejected in 24 hours. Verify your account now to keep your email active: mailbox-verify.example.com
scams.name: Mailbox Full Phishing Email
redFlags: Claims your mailbox is full or your password expires today
Threatens your email will be deleted or blocked
The sign-in link is not your real provider's website
The sender's address looks odd or misspelled
Generic greeting like 'Dear User' instead of your name
scams.summary: An email warns that your mailbox is full or your password is expiring, and incoming mail will be deleted unless you verify right away. The link opens a fake sign-in page that looks like your email provider and steals your password. With your email, scammers can reset your bank and shopping accounts too.
whatToDo: Do not click the link in the email
Open your email the normal way — type the address yourself or use your usual app
Check your storage there; if it is fine, the email was fake
Delete the email and mark it as phishing

scams.example: I recorded you through your webcam while you were on adult sites. I have the video and your contacts list. Send $1,200 in Bitcoin within 48 hours or I send it to everyone. I know your password is sunflower88.
scams.name: Webcam Blackmail Email
redFlags: Claims to have webcam video of you but shows no proof
Demands payment in Bitcoin with a deadline
Quotes an old password you used years ago
Threatens to send the 'video' to family and coworkers
Says they installed spyware or a 'remote desktop' program on your device
scams.summary: An email claims the sender hacked your webcam and filmed you doing something private, and demands bitcoin or the video goes to everyone you know. In almost every case there is no video and no hack — it is an empty threat sent to millions of people. Sometimes they include an old password from a years-old data leak to sound convincing.
whatToDo: Do not pay — there is almost never any video
Do not reply to the email
If they quoted a password you still use anywhere, change it and turn on two-factor authentication
Cover your webcam when not in use for peace of mind, and report the email as phishing

scams.example: Grandma, it's me — please don't tell Mom. I was in a car accident and I'm at the police station. I need $4,000 for bail right now. The officer will explain. Please hurry, I'm so scared.
scams.name: AI Voice Clone Family Emergency
redFlags: A family member calls from an unfamiliar number in a panic
Begs you not to tell anyone else
Needs bail, hospital, or tow money immediately
Someone else gets on the phone to give payment instructions
Wants gift cards, wire transfers, or cash picked up by a courier
scams.summary: Your phone rings and you hear what sounds exactly like your grandchild, child, or spouse — crying, hurt, arrested, or stranded and begging for bail or hospital money right away. The voice is generated by a computer from a few seconds of audio taken from social media videos. The emergency is not real; the money you send is gone.
whatToDo: Hang up and call the family member on the number you have saved for them
If you cannot reach them, call another relative and check before doing anything
Set a family code word only real family members would know
Never send money based on a phone call alone, no matter how real the voice sounds

scams.example: Missed call from +1 (268) 555-0142 at 2:14 AM. The number rang once and disconnected — it looks like a US area code but is actually an international premium number.
scams.name: One-Ring Callback Scam
redFlags: One ring, then the caller hangs up
Calls in the middle of the night
Area codes that look American but are actually Caribbean or international
Repeated one-ring calls from similar numbers
You do not recognize the number and know no one in that country
scams.summary: Your phone rings once in the middle of the night from an unfamiliar international number, then stops. It is bait: if you call back, you are connected to a premium-rate number overseas that charges a connection fee plus several dollars a minute while a recording keeps you on the line. The charge shows up on your phone bill.
whatToDo: Never call back an unfamiliar number that rang once
If it was a real call, the person will leave a message or call again
Check your phone bill for premium charges and dispute them with your carrier
Block the number and report it to your carrier

scams.example: ⚠ WARNING! Your computer has been locked due to a virus infection. Your photos and banking information are at risk. Call Microsoft Support immediately at 1-855-555-0167. Do not shut down your computer.
scams.name: Fake Virus Popup Warning
redFlags: A popup or voice warning says your computer is infected
It tells you to call a number immediately
It warns you not to shut down or restart
It uses Microsoft, Apple, or Windows logos on a web page
Real security software never asks you to call a phone number
signatures: do not shut down your computer
scams.summary: A loud full-screen popup freezes your browser claiming your computer is infected and your files or banking are at risk, with a number to call 'Microsoft' or 'Apple support' right away. It is just a web page. The people who answer are scammers who will ask for remote access and charge you hundreds of dollars to 'fix' a problem that does not exist.
whatToDo: Do not call the number and do not click anything in the popup
Close the browser — use Task Manager (Ctrl+Alt+Delete) or force-quit if it will not close
Restarting your computer is safe and usually makes the popup disappear
If you already let someone connect, disconnect from the internet and call your bank

scams.example: Great news! You qualify for the new Student Loan Forgiveness Program. Your balance of $38,000 can be eliminated. A processing fee of $499 reserves your spot — call 1-800-555-0134 before enrollment closes.
scams.name: Fake Student Loan Forgiveness
redFlags: Charges any fee for loan forgiveness or relief applications
Promises your loans will be forgiven immediately or completely
Pressures you to enroll before a deadline
Asks for your FSA ID username and password
Contacts you out of the blue by text, call, or social media ad
scams.summary: Ads, calls, and texts promise student loan forgiveness, relief, or a lowered payment — for an upfront or monthly fee. Applying for real federal loan programs is always free through the government and your loan servicer. These companies pocket the fee and do nothing, or worse, take your login and personal information.
whatToDo: Never pay for student loan help — real programs are free
Go directly to studentaid.gov or call your loan servicer at the number on your statement
Never share your FSA ID password with any company
Report the offer to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov

scams.example: Congratulations! You have been selected for a $5,000 National Merit Scholarship. To release your award, a federal processing tax of $180 is required. Provide payment within 7 days to claim your scholarship.
scams.name: Scholarship Fee Scam
redFlags: You 'won' a scholarship you never applied for
Requires a fee, tax, or payment to release the award
Asks for bank account details to 'deposit' the money
Guarantees everyone wins or is selected
Pressure to pay within days or lose it
signatures: you have been selected for a scholarship
scams.summary: A student gets a letter, email, or call saying they won a scholarship or grant they never applied for — they just have to pay a processing fee, a tax, or provide bank details for the deposit. Real scholarships never charge winners to collect. The 'award' vanishes once the fee is paid.
whatToDo: Never pay a fee to claim a scholarship or grant
Check the organization yourself — search its name plus 'scam'
Ask the school's financial aid office if the award is real
Report it to the FTC and your state attorney general

scams.example: Open enrollment ends soon! Get full health coverage for only $89 a month with no deductible. Press 1 now to speak with a licensed agent and lock in your rate before prices go up.
scams.name: Junk Health Plan Robocalls
redFlags: Unsolicited robocalls selling health insurance
Prices far cheaper than real plans with 'full coverage' promises
Pressure to sign up today before a deadline
They will not name the insurance company or send plan details in writing
Asks for Medicare, Social Security, or bank details on a cold call
scams.summary: During open enrollment, robocalls and ads push cheap 'health plans' that sound like real insurance. Many are thin discount plans or near-worthless policies that leave you uncovered when you get sick. Some callers only want your personal information to sign you up without permission or sell your data.
whatToDo: Hang up on robocall insurance sales
Shop only at healthcare.gov or through your state's official marketplace
Ask for the plan documents in writing and read what is actually covered
Never give Medicare or Social Security numbers to an unsolicited caller

scams.example: Cheap meds online — no prescription needed! Viagra, Tramadol, Insulin and more at 80% off US prices. Discreet shipping worldwide. Order now at bestmeds-cheap.example.com
scams.name: Rogue Online Pharmacy
redFlags: Sells prescription drugs with no prescription
Prices dramatically lower than every real pharmacy
No licensed pharmacist available to talk to
Ships from overseas with no physical address listed
Only accepts wire transfers, gift cards, or crypto
scams.summary: Websites advertise prescription drugs with no prescription needed, at prices far below any pharmacy. At best the pills never arrive; at worst you get counterfeit or dangerous medication — and your card details and health information are stolen for reuse. Legitimate online pharmacies always require a valid prescription.
whatToDo: Only buy from pharmacies that require a prescription
Check the pharmacy is licensed — look it up at the FDA's BeSafeRx page
Ask your regular pharmacist about discount programs instead
If you paid, report the charge to your card issuer and the site to the FDA

scams.example: Medicare is sending you 8 free COVID-19 test kits. Confirm your Medicare number and mailing address to receive your free kits this week: free-covid-kits.example.com
scams.name: Free COVID Test Kit Scam
redFlags: Anyone asks for your Medicare number to send 'free' tests
You receive boxes of tests you never ordered
Calls or texts offering free medical supplies out of the blue
They ask to 'confirm' your Medicare number or doctor's name
Medicare statements show tests you never took
scams.summary: Calls, texts, and ads offer free COVID test kits 'through Medicare' and ask for your Medicare number to ship them. The kits may arrive by the dozen or never come at all — the real product is your Medicare number, used to bill Medicare for tests you never ordered and to commit more fraud in your name.
whatToDo: Never give your Medicare number to an unsolicited caller or website
Order free tests only through official government channels or your pharmacy
Check your Medicare statements for tests you did not receive
Report Medicare fraud at 1-800-633-4227

scams.example: Medicare now covers a free DNA cancer screening for seniors. We will mail your kit today — just confirm your Medicare number and doctor's name so we can order your test: free-dna-screening.example.com
scams.name: Free DNA Testing Scam
redFlags: Offers 'free' genetic or cancer testing through Medicare
Recruiters at fairs, senior centers, or calling door to door
Asks for your Medicare number before any doctor is involved
Your own doctor never ordered or mentioned the test
Offers gift cards or cash for taking the test
scams.summary: At health fairs, by phone, or through ads, you are offered a 'free' genetic or cancer screening kit covered by Medicare — just swab your cheek and share your Medicare card. Real doctors did not order the test. The company bills Medicare thousands, harvests your ID for more fraud, and you may never see any results.
whatToDo: Do not accept genetic testing your own doctor did not order
Never share your Medicare number at a fair booth or with a cold caller
If a kit arrives unsolicited, do not use it — report it
Report Medicare fraud at 1-800-633-4227

scams.example: Watch the funeral service of Margaret E. live online. Register to view the livestream — a $1.99 verification payment is required to confirm your attendance: margaret-memorial-live.example.com
scams.name: Fake Funeral Livestream Scam
redFlags: A funeral livestream asks for any card payment
The link comes from a new or misspelled funeral home page
Asks for donations through gift cards or payment apps
The notice pressures you to register or pay quickly
The real funeral home's website has a different link or none at all
signatures: in loving memory join us online
donation in lieu of flowers via
scams.summary: Scammers copy real obituaries and post fake funeral notices and 'livestream' links on social media. Mourners who click are asked for card details to watch the service, or to send a 'donation' — the money goes to criminals exploiting a family's worst week. Real funeral homes do not charge guests to watch a livestream by card.
whatToDo: Never pay to watch a funeral livestream
Call the funeral home at its published number and ask for the real link
Send donations only through the family's chosen charity or the funeral home directly
Report the fake page to the social media platform

scams.example: We are relocating next month and would love you to care for our son. I am sending a check for $2,850 — keep $500 as your first week's pay and send the rest to our supplier for his wheelchair and supplies.
scams.name: Nanny Fake Check Scam
redFlags: Hired without an in-person meeting or interview
A check arrives before any work is done
You are told to send part of the money to someone else
Stories involve a deaf parent, a sick child, or an urgent relocation
Pay far above the going rate for sitting work
signatures: send the rest to our supplier
my husband and i are deaf
scams.summary: A 'family' hires you online as a nanny or sitter without ever meeting, then mails a large check to buy supplies, a wheelchair, or groceries before they 'move to town' — and asks you to send part of it on. The check is fake, the family does not exist, and your bank takes the full amount back from you.
whatToDo: Never deposit a check from an employer you have not met
Never send part of a check onward — that is always the scam
Wait for your bank to fully clear any check (weeks, not days) before spending it
Report the listing to the job site and stop contact

scams.example: Work from home as a Package Handler! Earn $2,400/month plus bonuses. Receive deliveries, inspect them, and reship with our prepaid labels. No experience needed — apply today and start this week.
scams.name: Package Reshipping Job Scam
redFlags: The job is just receiving and forwarding packages
Good pay for almost no described work
Packages arrive in other people's names
Labels and instructions come by email from a 'supervisor'
The company has no real office, phone number, or verifiable address
scams.summary: A work-from-home job pays you to receive packages and forward them to new addresses — 'quality inspection' or 'logistics' work. The packages were bought with stolen credit cards, and you are the middleman in a fraud ring. The paycheck never comes, and police may come asking questions about stolen goods passing through your home.
whatToDo: Never accept a job that involves reshipping merchandise
Stop receiving packages and contact the shipping company
Do not spend or send anything you already received
Report it to the FTC and your local police non-emergency line

scams.example: You did great in the interview — the position is yours! We are sending a check for $1,950 to set up your home office. Deposit it today and order your laptop and software from our vendor so you can start Monday.
scams.name: Fake Job Interview Scam
redFlags: The whole interview happens over text or chat, never by phone or video
You are hired unusually fast, sometimes the same day
A check arrives to buy equipment from their specific vendor
The job posting pays far above market for simple work
The company name is real but the email domain is slightly different
signatures: sending a check for your home office
you did great in the interview
scams.summary: A 'recruiter' interviews you entirely by text or chat for a job that sounds perfect, then 'hires' you on the spot. Next comes a check to buy a laptop and software from their 'approved vendor.' The check is fake, the vendor is the scammer, and you lose whatever you sent while your bank claws the check back.
whatToDo: Verify the job on the company's own website careers page
Call the company at its published number and confirm the recruiter works there
Real employers ship you equipment or buy it directly — never by check to you
Never deposit an equipment check or send money to a vendor

scams.example: Hey beautiful, I'm a successful businessman looking for a sugar baby. I'll send you $3,000 every week, no strings. I just sent your first payment — buy yourself something nice and send me a $200 gift card so I know you're serious.
scams.name: Sugar Daddy Allowance Scam
redFlags: A stranger offers large payments for little or nothing
The first payment is a check or a transfer that later bounces
You are asked to send gift cards or money back as a 'trust test'
They refuse video calls or meeting in public
Pressure and flattery whenever you hesitate
scams.summary: A wealthy stranger online offers a generous weekly 'allowance' just for your company or conversation. The first payment turns out to be a fake check or reversed transfer, and you are asked to send gift cards or part of the money back as a 'test of trust.' The allowance never existed — only your real money leaving ever happens.
whatToDo: Never send money or gift cards to someone who 'paid' you first
Assume any check or instant payment from a stranger can be reversed
Block the person and stop all contact
Report the profile on the app where they found you

scams.example: My dear, I see a dark curse over your family's money — that is why your luck has turned. I must cleanse the cash in a ritual for 9 nights. Bring me $5,000 in an envelope and I will return it blessed and doubled in luck.
scams.name: Psychic Curse Cleansing Scam
redFlags: A psychic discovers a curse, hex, or 'dark energy' on you or your money
The cleansing requires cash, jewelry, or gift cards handed over
Fees keep growing because the curse is 'stronger than expected'
You are told to keep the ritual secret from family
Promises your money or valuables will be returned 'blessed'
scams.summary: A fortune teller gives a cheap reading, then warns there is a curse on you or your money that only she can remove — for growing fees, sometimes demanding you hand over cash or jewelry to be 'cleansed' and returned. The curse is invented, and money handed over for cleansing is never seen again.
whatToDo: Never hand money or valuables to anyone for a ritual or cleansing
Stop all contact — a real advisor never demands secrecy and growing fees
If you already paid, report it to your local police; this is theft
Tell a family member, even if you were told to keep it secret

scams.example: Ad: '24/7 Locksmith — $19 service call, fast arrival!' After drilling your lock, the technician says: 'That will be $289 for the drilling plus $95 labor. Cash or card only — and there is a fee if you dispute it.'
scams.name: Bait-and-Switch Locksmith Scam
redFlags: Advertised prices like $19 that sound too good to be true
The business answers with a generic 'locksmith service' name
The technician insists your lock can only be drilled out
The final price is many times the quoted price
Demands cash and will not give a written invoice with a company name
signatures: we have to drill the lock
scams.summary: Locked out, you call the first locksmith ad promising a '$19 service call.' The person who arrives insists the lock must be drilled, and the final bill is hundreds of dollars, cash only, with threats if you refuse. The business is a call center using a fake local listing, not a real neighborhood locksmith.
whatToDo: Before any work, get the total price in writing and say no if it jumps
Ask for the business name, address, and license number before they start
Pick a locksmith before you need one — save a local shop's number after checking reviews
Report bait-and-switch pricing to your state attorney general

scams.example: NOTICE: Free water testing in your neighborhood this week! Our technician found contaminants in nearby homes. Sign up for your free test and qualify for a $500 rebate on a whole-home purification system.
scams.name: Free Water Test Filter Scam
redFlags: Free water testing offered by postcard, phone, or door-to-door
Scary on-the-spot demonstrations showing your water is 'contaminated'
Same-day pressure to sign for a system costing thousands
Financing paperwork rushed in front of you at the kitchen table
The 'rebate' or discount is only good if you sign today
signatures: sign up today for your free test
scams.summary: A postcard or door-knocker offers a free water quality test. The 'test' uses chemical tricks that make any tap water look contaminated, scaring you into a filtration system costing thousands on a long payment plan. Your water was almost certainly fine, and the same filters sell for a fraction of the price elsewhere.
whatToDo: Do not sign anything the same day — legitimate offers survive a night's sleep
Get a real test from your water utility or an independent certified lab
Ask your city for its free annual water quality report
Remember you usually have 3 business days to cancel a door-to-door sale — use it

scams.example: Afternoon! We're paving up the street and have hot asphalt left over that'll just go to waste. We can do your whole driveway today for $800 cash — half the normal price — but we need a yes in the next 30 minutes.
scams.name: Leftover Asphalt Paving Scam
redFlags: A crew appears uninvited with a 'leftover materials' story
Cash price, today only, decision needed in minutes
No written contract, business card, or license number
Out-of-state plates and no local address
Price jumps once the old driveway is torn up
scams.summary: A crew knocks saying they just finished a job nearby and have leftover asphalt — they will pave your driveway cheap, today only, cash price. The work is thin, unsealed, and washes away within months, or the price triples once they start. Real paving companies do not sell leftovers door to door.
whatToDo: Say no to any unsolicited paving offer, however good it sounds
Get three written quotes from local companies with real addresses
Never pay cash in advance for driveway work
Report traveling paving crews to your local police non-emergency line

scams.example: We're in the area doing storm repairs — we can inspect your roof free today and handle your insurance claim for you. Just sign this authorization and pay a $1,500 deposit so we can schedule you first, before the next rain.
scams.name: Storm Chaser Roofing Scam
redFlags: Crews appear at your door right after a storm
Out-of-state plates, no local office or address
Pressure to sign an 'authorization' or assignment of insurance benefits
Deposit demanded in cash or by check before any work
No permits, no written contract, no warranty paperwork
scams.summary: After a storm, out-of-state crews go door to door offering free roof inspections and fast repairs. Some take a deposit and never return; others do sloppy work with no permits or warranty, and are gone before the leaks start. Your signature on their paperwork may also hand them control of your insurance claim.
whatToDo: Do not sign anything or pay a deposit at your door
Call your insurance company yourself and ask how to file a claim
Use a local, licensed roofer with a real office and references
Get the full contract in writing, including materials, permits, and cleanup

emergency.label: Bank transfer or wire
steps: Call your bank RIGHT NOW at the number on your card or statement. Ask for the fraud department and a transfer recall. Minutes matter - same-day recalls sometimes work.
If you cannot reach them by phone, go to a branch in person.
Report it at reportfraud.ftc.gov and ic3.gov.
Write down everything - times, names, phone numbers - while it is fresh.

emergency.label: Zelle, Cash App, or Venmo
steps: Call your bank immediately. These payments move fast and are hard to reverse, but some banks now reimburse certain imposter scams - always ask.
Report the scam inside the payment app as well.
Report it at reportfraud.ftc.gov and ic3.gov.
Do NOT pay anyone who contacts you offering to 'recover' the money for a fee. That is a second scam aimed at victims.

emergency.label: Gift cards
steps: Call the number on the back of the card RIGHT NOW. If the money has not been spent yet, the issuer can sometimes freeze it.
Keep the card and the store receipt - you will need both.
Report it at reportfraud.ftc.gov. The FTC uses these reports, and some issuers give refunds.
Tell the store where you bought the cards - some stores will flag the purchase.

emergency.label: Cryptocurrency
steps: Be clear-eyed: crypto transfers usually cannot be reversed. Documentation matters more than speed now.
Save everything: wallet addresses, transaction IDs, chats, and screenshots.
Report it to the FBI at ic3.gov and at reportfraud.ftc.gov. Large cases do get investigated.
NEVER pay a 'recovery service' that contacts you. Recovery scams are an entire second industry built on victims.

emergency.label: Credit or debit card
steps: Call the number on the back of the card and dispute the charge. Credit cards have the strongest protections on this whole list.
If you gave the card number to a scammer, ask for a new card number.
Check your statement for small test charges you do not recognize.
Report it at reportfraud.ftc.gov.

emergency.label: Cash, check, or mail
steps: If you mailed a check that has not been cashed, call your bank and stop payment.
If cash went through the mail, call the U.S. Postal Inspection Service at 1-877-876-2455.
If a courier picked up cash, call your local police non-emergency line and file a report. It matters.
Report it at reportfraud.ftc.gov and ic3.gov.
